The lack of broad local involvement under this planning system has hindered the establishment of widespread local support for wind power projects.

10. ID: 1894
   Year: 2007
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: PlanEnergi
   Statement: We believe the Samsø Energy Island project must be regarded as a near-complete success. Our primary objective—achieving 100% self-sufficiency with renewable energy using local resources—has been accomplished. This achievement includes the total elimination of CO₂ emissions and other air pollutants. A key factor behind this success is the active mobilization and support of the local community, who embraced and adopted the project.

However, not all conservation objectives have been met. In particular, goals related to heating and electricity efficiency were not fully achieved, and transportation remains largely unchanged, still dependent on non-renewable energy sources.

This project was an enormous undertaking for a small community, yet they completed it on schedule. But could the same be done on a national scale? There are significant challenges to consider. National energy consumption per capita is 25% higher than that of Samsø. Additionally, Denmark has only one-third of the biomass resources per capita compared to Samsø, and the national wind resource potential per person is also lower.

If Samsø’s contribution is viewed as part of Denmark's national renewable energy (RE) supply, two scenarios emerge:

If based on Samsø’s land and resource capacity, RE production would need to increase fourfold.
If based on Samsø’s population proportion, RE production must increase by 25%.
In either case, a significant increase in renewable energy production would be required. These observations are not intended to diminish Samsø’s achievements but to provide perspective on the scale of a national transition to renewable energy.

One crucial conclusion is clear: if Denmark aims to make a similar transition, substantial energy conservation efforts are necessary to reduce overall energy consumption. Samsø’s experience demonstrates that these savings will not happen automatically—it will require substantial effort, supported by economic incentives and penalties. Importantly, every kilowatt-hour saved is more valuable than one produced—it requires no maintenance or service.

A direct application of Samsø’s results to Denmark indicates that transitioning to a renewable energy system nationwide would require an investment of approximately 670 billion DKK (89 billion EUR). However, this transition could yield annual savings of around 60 billion DKK (8 billion EUR), allowing the investment to pay off in just 11 years—a promising return, given the gravity of the challenge and the potential benefits.

14. ID: 5719
   Year: 2009
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Jochen Markard ,  Regula Petersen
   Statement: Offshore wind power has transformed the wind energy sector by leveraging open sea space and strong wind speeds for large-scale electricity generation. However, it is a capital-intensive and technologically demanding industry, requiring financial and organizational resources that exclude many smaller investors. Our analysis of offshore wind park ownership in Denmark, the UK, and Germany reveals that large firms, particularly from the electricity sector, dominate investments. In Denmark and the UK, oil and gas industry players also play a significant role in offshore wind development. 

This marks a major shift for countries like Germany and Denmark, where the wind power sector initially thrived on investments from individuals, farmers, cooperatives, and independent developers. The rise of offshore wind thus signifies a transition toward market concentration and a departure from the inclusive investment model that previously characterized these countries' renewable energy landscapes.

16. ID: 4018
   Year: 2010
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The Danish government has submitted a national action plan to the EU Commission, confirming that Denmark is on track to meet its renewable energy goals for 2020. The targets include sourcing at least 30% of total energy consumption from renewable energy and ensuring that 10% of the energy used in the transport sector comes from renewable sources. To achieve this, Denmark plans to significantly increase its wind power capacity and transition large power plants from coal to biomass.

The government’s action plan outlines the steps already taken and highlights additional measures that will be introduced as part of a new energy agreement for the period after 2011. Climate Minister Lykke Friis expressed confidence that, with existing initiatives, Denmark is nearly there, and emphasized upcoming discussions on how to reach the final steps toward these goals. Additionally, the Danish Climate Commission is expected to release a report in September detailing how Denmark can achieve independence from fossil fuels.

The Danish Energy Agency's projections suggest that by 2020, Denmark will achieve a renewable energy share of 28.3%, and 6% of energy used in transport will be renewable, though these projections are subject to uncertainty. The government is required to submit biannual progress reports to the EU to demonstrate that Denmark is on track to meet its targets. If there is a delay in meeting these goals, the government must take additional action to ensure progress.

20. ID: 349
   Year: 2011
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Soren Hermansen
   Statement: Our success on Samsø Island proves that the transition to renewable energy can work when we involve citizens directly. Let me be clear: The EU's targets for CO2 reduction and renewable energy are fine, but what matters is the practical implementation. In 1998, we took on the challenge of transforming Samsø to 100% renewable energy in just 10 years - and we succeeded. The key was making local citizens part-owners in the projects.

From my experience on Samsø, I can tell you that people view wind turbines much more favorably when they have ownership stakes. When energy savings flow directly to people's own pockets, they become enthusiastic participants. Denmark's feed-in tariffs and progressive planning policies made this possible.

During Denmark's EU presidency, we must emphasize that setting visions isn't enough - we need binding targets, realistic budgets, and practical policies that reward participation. The global climate negotiations aren't producing results fast enough. Instead of waiting for global agreements, the EU should follow Denmark's model of green growth policies that create jobs and innovation while reducing emissions.

The solution is to make climate action personally relevant to citizens through cooperative ownership and financial incentives. Citizens should face consequences for wasteful energy use but receive rewards for supporting green initiatives. We can't wait for governments alone to solve climate change - we need to empower citizens to take action now through proven approaches like we used on Samsø.

25. ID: 2376
   Year: 2012
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Researchers
   Statement: The increasing threat of climate change has spurred a global movement towards low-carbon living, including the development of low-carbon cities and communities. However, building a truly low-carbon island presents significant challenges. It requires a holistic approach that considers the intricate interplay of various factors, including population, land use, industrial activity, transportation patterns, and energy consumption habits. 

To effectively evaluate the impact of low-carbon initiatives, such as the green transportation policy in the Penghu Low Carbon Island Development Project, a robust and reliable assessment framework is crucial. We believe that a system dynamics approach offers a valuable tool for understanding the complex interactions between different factors within the island's transportation system. By developing a dynamic model that incorporates key variables like population, tourism, electric scooter usage, government subsidies, and motorcycle licensing restrictions, we can simulate the potential effects of the green transportation policy and gain valuable insights into the evolving behavior of the transportation system under different policy scenarios.

31. ID: 5757
   Year: 2015
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Til Kristian Vrana
   Statement: The electrical installations for offshore wind power plants are currently built above sea level. We know that the necessary substructure for a transformer or converter platform becomes more costly with increasing water depth and mass. Therefore, we believe the main challenges are the hydrostatic pressure, the rough sea environment, and the extreme reliability requirements, as maintenance is very complicated at the seabed. Subsea technology has not been seen as crucially important for offshore wind, where water depths are usually less than 50m. However, we believe that subsea technology might find its way into the offshore wind sector, possibly leading to transformer stations or even converter stations being placed on the seabed. Therefore, we find it necessary to investigate the possibilities and potentials of the subsea approach.

As we have observed a steadily increasing share of HVDC components in the European power grid, making this approach is becoming outdated. 
We propose that control philosophies for hybrid AC+DC grids have to be developed, as these can address the future reality much better than the classical AC approach. We think the North Sea region with its very high concentration of HVDC infrastructure is a perfect case for studying hybrid AC+DC grid control. We believe the North Sea region will significantly benefit from improved operational principles.

We know that protection of large HVDC systems is challenging. Protection schemes including fast fault location for selective fault clearing are still work in progress. In the report we have illustrated two different approaches: adapting AC protection strategies to work for DC (TRL3-5) or completely new DC power system protection (TRL 1-3). The protection components, both circuit breakers and fault current limiters, are immature at the moment. Although we know HVDC breaker prototypes have been successfully developed, the performance has never been tested in a real HVDC system, which will be a challenge. We believe the optimal HVDC converter control in case of a DC fault is not yet known and possibly depends on converter topology. We find the design of the complex protection system needs further development, before implementation. We urge the stakeholders to investigate alternative protection concepts compared to the classical AC-inspired protection approaches.

We believe low Frequency AC (LFAC) technology has to be further studied with regards to its use for integrating medium-distance offshore wind power plants. For near-shore WPPs (less than ca. 100 km from shore), we believe regular AC is normally the best choice, and for remote offshore WPPs (more than ca. 100 km from shore) we believe DC is usually the best choice. 
For WPPs with an intermediate distance (ca. 50-150 km from shore) we believe LFAC might offer benefits, then the two already mentioned options. We find that LFAC approach also poses a serious threat for the establishment of a future North Sea Super Grid, as it pushes the limits of how far offshore we can go with AC technology. We have showcased in this report that many of the future offshore wind power plants needs to be integrated with LFAC instead of HVDC, as the number of HVDC connected facilities is reduced. We believe a smaller total number of relevant facilities might reduce the incentives and benefits to consider a HVDC based North Sea Super Grid.

We found during our investigation of that operating and controlling HVDC connected isolated offshore AC systems is challenging, as these are highly important for offshore supernodes and therefore can be an enabler for the NSSG. Present offshore grid studies have focused on grid topologies and detailed cable planning. However, we believe that integrated storage has not been considered enough in this context. We see a need for more research within these areas specific on the added value of placing storage units offshore and considering placement in a meshed grid HVDC structure. We think it would be a very large step to take the decision to now build a full-scale North Sea Super Grid, as more investigation into its constructed is needed as outlined in this report.

32. ID: 3163

   Statement: Lund University highlights the growing priority of transitioning from fossil fuel-based to renewable energy systems, which has led to an increase in renewable energy investments. However, this shift raises critical concerns regarding the sustainability of energy governance, particularly in relation to access, control, public participation, and transparency. Community renewable energy projects empower communities to act as citizens instead of just consumers. Lund University examines how these projects, as seen in Feldheim (Germany) and Samsø (Denmark), reflect local, communitarian ecological citizenship focused on community interests like economic development rather than global sustainability goals like climate change. The study also explores the role of intentionality in achieving ecological outcomes in renewable energy transitions.

37. ID: 5732
   Year: 2016
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Researchers
   Statement: The offshore grid has unique technical, economic, and social characteristics, requiring different research methodologies for various questions. Net social benefits at a regional level generally increase with higher offshore wind capacities and more integrated grids. The grid can provide benefits such as more efficient dispatch, better wind power connection, increased system flexibility and reliability, and interconnection of power markets and Nordic storage.

A meshed grid typology may enhance these benefits compared to a radial one, requiring less investment and reducing offshore wind curtailment, along with other non-monetary benefits. However, a meshed grid without proper cost and benefit allocation creates winners and losers among North Seas countries and their neighbors. The offshore grid involves unproven technology, especially control strategies and large HVDC breakers, and an integrated grid could require greater investments than a radial one.

There are significant technical, governance, and regulatory challenges for a meshed grid, which in some studies show only marginally greater benefits than a radial solution. Studies indicate the offshore grid will develop gradually, starting with national shared transmission and bilateral interconnector projects, followed by international pilot projects, and eventually more complex ones.

Our island’s economic growth is closely tied to tourism, so maintaining the natural beauty of our land is crucial. While aesthetically acceptable designs are important for energy generation plants, their appearance ranks as the least important operational criterion when we evaluate renewable energy applications. Environmental protection is our top priority, with 44% of us ranking it highest, followed by cost (18.6%), energy efficiency (17%), and operational safety (13.7%). The appearance of the technology, as well as the size and noise of the structures, hold secondary importance.  

Despite the need for aesthetic improvements to enhance social acceptance, we emphasize that environmental protection and efficiency are the primary considerations for renewable energy systems on our island.

56. ID: 2590
   Year: 2017
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Karl Sperling
   Statement: Denmark's success with community energy projects, particularly on Samsø Island, isn't just about the end results - it's about understanding HOW we achieved those results. My colleagues and I at Aalborg University believe that the success of Samsø's transformation to renewable energy depended on specific external and internal conditions that must be understood before attempting to replicate this model elsewhere.

The external factors that made Samsø successful included clear national energy policies, government funding programs for renewable energy, and expert technical consultation. But equally important were the internal community factors: Samsø's history of agricultural cooperatives, a strong sense of community responsibility, and experienced local tradespeople who had worked with wind turbines since the 1980s.

The key to success was alignment between these external and internal factors. Our Renewable Energy Island Master Plan translated national goals into local action. Our project manager, Søren Hermansen, was crucial in integrating renewable energy goals into community life. This wasn't just about local ownership of energy infrastructure - it was about deep community integration.

For policymakers looking to replicate Samsø's success, my message is clear: having the right framework conditions isn't enough. You must make time and space for community interests to align with renewable energy targets. Success depends on supporting local mediators who can bridge the gap between national policy and community needs.

The project focused on addressing the real challenges faced by small islands, such as securing reliable, year-round energy supplies from wind and solar sources, and developing advanced electricity storage and distribution systems for both local and central requirements.

Public tendering for offshore wind in Denmark has introduced nearshore wind farms as an alternative for reducing costs. 78. ID: 4016
   Year: 2019
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Martin Skov Skjøth-Rasmussen
   Statement: At Haldor Topsøe, we are working on a completely different approach to energy storage than the commonly discussed batteries. We focus on storing energy in chemicals such as hydrogen, methane, methanol, and ammonia, which can be used as fuel. This is where our expertise in electrolysis comes into play.

Electrolysis allows us to use excess electricity from wind turbines or solar panels to split water vapor (H2O) into oxygen and hydrogen in an electrolyzer. The hydrogen we produce can then be used for various purposes, including the production of ammonia (NH3) or upgrading biogas to natural gas (methane, CH4) by reacting the CO2 in the biogas with the hydrogen.

This process effectively stores the electrical energy as chemical energy, which can later be used as fuel for heavy transport, such as trucks and ships. In Denmark, I see enormous potential in upgrading biogas to natural gas, as we already have an extensive natural gas network and significant biogas resources, largely due to our substantial agricultural production.

Biogas contains about 30-40 percent CO2, and by upgrading it to natural gas, we can save considerable amounts of CO2 while also utilizing the CO2 as energy. In the long term, the biogas resources we have in Denmark could nearly replace the natural gas we currently extract from the North Sea. This represents a major step forward in reducing CO2 emissions and optimizing the use of our renewable energy resources.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

81. ID: 4268
   Year: 2019
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: Dan Jørgensen
   Statement: Denmark's government is planning a groundbreaking energy project: an artificial island surrounded by massive offshore wind farms. This energy island will be revolutionary in its ability to convert and store renewable electricity at an unprecedented scale. The project will cost between 200-300 billion Danish kroner (approximately 27-40 billion euros) and will be operational before 2030.

The surrounding wind farms will have a combined peak capacity of 10 gigawatts - equivalent to about 1,000 of today's most powerful offshore wind turbines and far exceeding the current largest offshore plant of 1.2 gigawatts. The generated electricity will be enough to power 10 million households, which is more than Denmark's entire population. The power will be transmitted to the artificial island via underwater cables and converted into storable energy forms like hydrogen, synthetic fuels, or gas using Power-to-X technologies.

The site selection and approval process should be completed by 2021, followed by construction. While there are significant technical challenges for such a large offshore project, and Power-to-X technology is currently expensive, the massive scale of these planned facilities should lead to dramatic cost reductions.

This energy island is central to Denmark's climate strategy. Under the new Climate Act passed by our Social Democratic government coalition, Denmark must cut greenhouse gas emissions by 70% by 2030, aiming for complete climate neutrality by 2050. Denmark's power grid will run on 100% renewable energy by 2028.

We have initiated a new era for offshore wind with energy islands in Denmark, including the decision to advance the Hesselø Offshore Wind Farm (800-1,200 MW) and two energy islands - one in the North Sea and one on Bornholm - with a total of 5 GW connected initially, and the potential for 10 GW in the North Sea later.

The Bornholm energy island project alone will generate 2 GW by 2030, producing more electricity than Bornholm's entire annual consumption. Profitability of these energy islands depends on securing adequate sales opportunities for the green electricity produced. Given these massive state-planned expansions, it would be inappropriate to lift the state's area reservations now.

Regarding local ownership, I cannot support increasing the buyer's rights scheme from 20% to 50% local ownership. The Justice Ministry previously found that even a 33.3% mandatory local ownership would violate EU's right of establishment and make Denmark less attractive for wind development. Moreover, we have actually terminated the buyer's rights scheme as of June 1, 2020, as analysis showed it failed to increase local acceptance of wind projects. We have replaced it with a RE-bonus and a green pool system.

I also cannot support providing state guarantees for project development under the open-door scheme, as this would mean the state taking on unlimited risk without project control. The state should only bear development risks for projects it initiates through tenders.

117. ID: 689
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Dan Jørgensen
   Statement: Q: Can the minister confirm that the potential for the so-called Power-to-X (PtX) products and energy storage is relatively limited before 2030? If so, could the minister explain what this means for the profitability of the project regarding the establishment of an "energy island"?

A: Regarding the establishment of one or more potential energy islands, the spread of PtX production could lead to synergies due to a more efficient utilization of the island's offshore wind production. This is partly because hydrogen production via electrolysis can consume electricity more flexibly and intermittently than other types of consumption. Thus, electrolysis can occur when offshore wind electricity is abundant and cheap, and conversely, it can be disconnected during shortages. If a flexible electrolysis plant is integrated with an energy island and placed in the same location on the grid as the island’s offshore wind production, the need for extensive upgrades to the transmission grid could be reduced, as the plant could act as a "buffer" between large-scale RE electricity production and the grid.

The use of PtX production in conjunction with an energy island could thus raise the threshold for how much RE can be efficiently integrated into Denmark’s energy system. The larger the capacity of flexible PtX production placed in the same location on the grid as the island’s offshore wind production, the more offshore wind capacity can be connected to and landed from the island, thereby increasing the value of offshore wind production, relieving the electricity transmission grid, and reducing the need for internal grid upgrades. Therefore, we must consider the possibility of developing potential energy islands in phases as Denmark also scales up and potentially accelerates PtX production and demand.

122. ID: 2827
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: Job creation and innovation
   Actor: Jakob Nørmark
   Statement: As Bornholms Tidende, I can tell you that the construction of offshore wind farms connected to an energy island/hub is possible in all the investigated areas, including 10 gigawatts in the three areas in the North Sea and 3 gigawatts in Bornholm I+II. The screening found a total capacity of 18 gigawatts. However, for the areas in the Baltic Sea, it is recommended that a more detailed analysis of the sensitivity of selected bird species be conducted, and consideration should be given to cables, pipelines, and existing shipping routes.

The cost of constructing offshore wind farms near Bornholm with a total capacity of 3 gigawatts is estimated at 58.26 billion Danish kroner. This is approximately 370 million kroner cheaper than the calculated investments for 3 gigawatts in the North Sea energy island project, with a price difference of less than 1%. Utilizing Bornholm's solid ground avoids the 3.6 billion kroner expense for establishing an energy island, which is only included in the North Sea calculation. However, the expenses for new export cables to Zealand and Poland for Bornholm are valued at 23.7 billion kroner, which is 6.7 billion kroner more than the cable expenses in the North Sea.

The long-term expenses relative to the amount of electricity produced indicate that it appears to be more cost-effective to invest in the North Sea. The North Sea project is more efficient than the Bornholm project due to a better wind resource and cheaper export connections. The wind blows at 10.73 meters per second in the North Sea, while it averages 9.92 meters per second south of Bornholm.

The western part of Bornholm II is located in an internationally important bird area, where long-tailed ducks, velvet scoters, and common scoters overwinter. There is a risk that these species will be displaced from an important foraging area if offshore wind turbines are installed. Additionally, the Baltic Sea area between Denmark, Sweden, and Germany is important for crane and raptor migration. Bornholm I and II lie in the migration routes for birds that breed in Sweden and Norway and overwinter to the south.

The seabed in the two Bornholm fields is rated as "less suitable" compared to the North Sea areas. The area is considered less suitable for foundation with monopiles due to the possible presence of hard clay with stones, high-lying hard and flint-rich chalk, and high-lying, possibly cemented marine deposits. However, no geological or geotechnical factors have been found that would prevent the placement of offshore wind turbine foundations.

The two Danish power grids have limited capacity. Due to the capacity ceiling, it is assumed that only 1 gigawatt produced at Bornholm will go to the Danish grid, while the remaining 1-2 gigawatts will be sent abroad, likely through the proposed connection to Poland.

In the wind turbines, alternating current is produced with a voltage of 66 kilovolts. Transformer platforms will be built at sea near the wind turbines, where the voltage will be raised to 220 kilovolts. From there, parallel cable systems, each with a total installed capacity of 500 megawatts, will be built. If 2 gigawatts are installed, four export cables must be brought ashore, where a transformer station near the coast converts the alternating current to direct current.

An area just north of Hasle has been designated as the location where the power will be brought ashore. Energinet has identified an area of 4-6 hectares where there is room for the facility. However, the location of the onshore facility could be moved along the coast, depending on the preliminary project.

135. ID: 2610

   Statement: The Danish “Energy Island” project involves creating an offshore hub that connects 12 GW of offshore wind farms and interconnection capacity between Denmark, the Netherlands, and Germany. Market design decisions, including ownership and remuneration structures, are vital to ensure fairness and economic viability for all countries involved.

   Statement: Kraka’s report also discusses long-term electricity prices and project economics. Here, I would like to note that there is inherent uncertainty about the future—especially for a project of the size and duration of the North Sea Energy Island. This uncertainty particularly applies to electricity price projections. However, uncertainty is not an argument against making decisions, which I note Kraka also acknowledges in its report. Instead, we strive to mitigate risks continuously. One way is to diversify risks by, for example, allowing room for innovation and expanding the island's portfolio, such as supporting the production and distribution of hydrogen or other green gases from the island, or supporting other large-scale consumers like data centers.

Another way to spread risk is through the choice of ownership model. In the agreement, we decided that the project would be based on shared ownership, with the state owning 50.1% of the island and a private partner owning 49.9%. The private co-owner will be selected through a competitive tender process. Shared ownership has the advantage that the island's economics are market-tested, and the risk is shared, as both parties bear the subsequent financial responsibilities of the project.

154. ID: 168
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: Dan Jørgensen
   Statement: I, on behalf of the Danish Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities, outlines the vision and strategic priorities for the energy island concept. An energy island is designed to serve as a hub for offshore wind energy production, enabling efficient use of offshore wind potential far from the coast while integrating significantly more renewable energy into the European energy system—a critical step for the green transition. The island will connect nearby offshore wind farms, distributing electricity directly to multiple countries via export cables, which also reduce the need for onshore infrastructure investments by serving as both landing and trading cables. This dual functionality can lead to significant cost savings and minimizes the need for expanding Denmark's onshore grid.

However, realizing these benefits requires addressing challenges such as the historically long development times for export connections, which can take 8–9 years. Political agreements with relevant neighboring countries need to be finalized promptly to ensure the energy island project can be completed by 2030. To support this initiative, 65 million DKK was allocated in the 2020 Finance Act for preliminary investigations, including 26 million DKK for fine-screening suitable locations based on environmental, natural, and planning factors. These analyses will also evaluate the economic feasibility of the project and the role of export connections in ensuring profitability.

In parallel, the Ministry has initiated informal dialogues with North Sea countries to explore collaborative opportunities, further ensuring that the energy island project is positioned as a cornerstone for both Denmark's and Europe's renewable energy future.

157. ID: 1521
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Ole Graa Jakobsen
   Statement: Mærsk about Power-to-X:
"A.P. Møller-Mærsk, as the world’s largest container shipping company with around 700 vessels, is actively pursuing alternative fuels to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050. We see electrofuels as a promising substitute for fossil-based bunker oil, alongside fuels derived from biomass. Currently, it is too early to commit to a single future fuel type, but the transition must accelerate to meet our goals. 

Mærsk has partnered with Ørsted, DSV, DFDS, Copenhagen Airport, and SAS to develop a 1.3 GW Power-to-X facility near Copenhagen by 2030 for producing hydrogen and other sustainable fuels. As end-users, we are focused on identifying the modifications required for our ships to use electrofuels and the necessary adjustments across the bunkering system and supply chain to facilitate the transition.

Even with a fully operational 1.3 GW plant, the facility would supply only a small fraction of our fleet's needs. Scaling this effort globally for the entire shipping industry would require approximately 1,000 plants of this size. Despite this, we see the Copenhagen project as a critical starting point, helping to kickstart electrofuel production in Denmark and potentially positioning Denmark as a global leader in this field. Denmark's strengths in wind energy and advanced Power-to-X technologies make it uniquely positioned to lead this transition.

However, significant investments will be required to retrofit ships and adapt supply chains. The greater challenge lies in developing these new fuels and building the infrastructure to produce them. To overcome this, we need incentives, such as a carbon tax on fossil fuels, to offset the higher cost of green fuels. Additionally, Mærsk is working to reduce fuel consumption and improve efficiency, aiming to cut CO2 emissions per container transported by 60% by 2030 compared to 2008 levels."

164. ID: 7010
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Alessandro Singlitico, Nicolas Jean Bernard Campion, Marie Münster, Matti Juhani Koivisto, Nicolaos Antonio Cutululis, Cathy Jingqing Suo, Kenneth Karlsson, Torben Jørgensen, Jeppe Eimose Waagstein, Maja F. Bendtsen
   Statement: Bornholm has the potential to become the first natural energy hub in the Baltic Sea due to its strategic position for offshore wind power expansion, planned energy interconnections, and the need for storing and converting surplus power. Bornholm could serve as both a center for electrical equipment, including substations and connection nodes between countries, and a hub for power-to-x (P2X) production using offshore wind power.
A preliminary investigation shows that placing an electrolyser in Bornholm would result in lower hydrogen production costs than placing it in Copenhagen. However, Bornholm faces limitations, including restricted access to carbon dioxide (CO2), oxygen (O2), and heat consumers. The CO2 available from combined heat and power (CHP) plants burning biomass and biogas production from all digestible wet feedstocks would be insufficient to meet Rønne Havn's demand for renewable fuels.
To achieve immediate decarbonization of the maritime transport sector, converting hydrogen into a drop-in fuel is necessary, with methanol being the most promising alternative. However, the CO2 available from biomass combustion and biogas production is insufficient to meet the methanol demand of ferries, covering only about half of the requirement.
The lowest methanol production cost, calculated at €589 per tonne, occurs when the electrolyser is located on Bornholm, has access to the public grid, faces no CO2 limitations, and all by-products (heat and oxygen) are sold. Conversely, placing an electrolyser in Copenhagen would result in higher hydrogen production costs due to elevated grid connection expenses and the higher cost of electricity delivered onshore from offshore wind power plants (OWPP). 
For optimal cost efficiency, a large share of the electricity consumed by the electrolyser would need to come from the public grid, as the price of grid electricity is often lower than the cost of delivering offshore wind power onshore. However, due to Bornholm's resource limitations, Copenhagen could become a more favorable location if CO2 is available in sufficient quantities and all by-products can be sold without restrictions.
Producing hydrogen offshore without the ability to sell by-products is the most expensive option. Increasing system flexibility would significantly improve the economic potential of offshore electrolysers.

198. ID: 2757
   Year: 2020
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Ministry of Finance
   Statement: As the Ministry of Finance, we fully support the Danish government's climate action plan, which includes a series of ambitious initiatives aimed at significantly reducing CO2 emissions by 2030. Our focus is on financing and supporting critical projects that drive Denmark's transition to greener energy.

Regarding the two energy islands, Denmark will lead the world by establishing energy islands to harness offshore wind resources far from the coast. These islands will not only make wind energy production more efficient but also reduce the need for new land-based power infrastructure. Two energy islands will be established by 2030, one in the North Sea and one in the Baltic Sea, with each having a capacity of 2 GW initially, and a potential to scale to 10 GW.

The plan also allocates 400 million Danish kroner annually to support the capture and storage of CO2 from industries, as well as the development of green fuels through large-scale Power-to-X (PtX) facilities. These initiatives will help reduce industrial carbon footprints and enable green energy to be converted into fuels for sectors like aviation and transport.

We also recognize the need to improve energy efficiency in buildings and industries. The government will enhance energy labeling, create a better decision-making basis for property owners, and focus on improving industrial energy use. We are setting aside 900 million Danish kroner to promote electrification and energy efficiency in industries from 2020 to 2024.

Additionally, we will invest in green district heating, replacing oil and gas with sustainable alternatives. We plan to reduce taxes on green electricity for heating while increasing taxes on fossil fuels, and provide subsidies for heat pumps and green waste heat from data centers.

Finally, our vision includes a climate-neutral waste sector by 2030, with a significant reduction in the burning of plastic and an increase in recycling. This will contribute to the overall reduction in Denmark's carbon footprint.

The Ministry of Finance will ensure that these ambitious measures are financially supported, contributing to Denmark's goal of a sustainable, low-carbon economy.

202. ID: 2531
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Dr. Naveed Akhtar
   Statement: The expansion of wind energy in the German Bight and the Baltic Sea has accelerated, with wind turbines generating around 8,000 megawatts, equivalent to eight nuclear power plants. However, space is limited, leading to wind farms being built close together. My team found that wind speeds at downstream wind farms are significantly slowed, creating large-scale low wind patterns extending 35 to 40 kilometers, and up to 100 kilometers in certain weather conditions. This reduces the output of neighboring wind farms by 20 to 25 percent, causing economic consequences. Future planning must consider these wake effects.

We used the COSMO-CLM computer model to assess future wind characteristics for offshore expansion, combining it with future wind farm characteristics. Our study is based on the 2015 wind farm planning for the North Sea, which includes some wind farms not yet built.

222. ID: 1792

   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Chairman of the new association "Atomkraft Ja Tak"
   Statement: I’ve done some calculations on how much energy this energy island will generate over its entire lifespan. It will produce enough electricity to cover Denmark’s electricity consumption for 30 years. 

If, instead, we had built a standard nuclear power plant for the same amount of money, we could have generated enough electricity to cover our consumption for 114 years, and we would also have gotten free district heating on the side, enough to supply all of our district heating for 114 years as well. 

We often hear that this island will deliver 10 gigawatts. That’s the capacity, but the wind doesn’t blow all the time, so in reality, it will only generate about 4.5 gigawatts once you account for the fact that it’s not always windy. 

For the same money, you could have gotten approximately 7 gigawatts of nuclear power, which produces a steady output continuously.

268. ID: 1008
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: NCCS, LowEmission and NTRANS
   Statement: Energy islands, also known as energy hubs, are poised to become a critical component of the North Sea's green transition infrastructure. These energy hubs will act as central connecting points for offshore wind farms, linking the wind farms to land through the international subsea grid. The energy hubs can house facilities for producing zero-emission fuels, utilizing surplus wind energy to store energy as ammonia or hydrogen. Additionally, they could enable the production of blue hydrogen with integrated carbon capture and storage technology, injecting the captured CO₂ into nearby disused oil wells beneath the seabed. Beyond fuel production, energy hubs could distribute zero-carbon fuels to passing ships for refueling or to tankers for transport to land. They may also serve as command centers for offshore wind installation and maintenance activities, as well as provide charging points for battery-powered ships.

281. ID: 1209
   Year: 2021

   Statement: Denmark's government has agreed to take a 51% stake in a £25bn artificial "energy island" to be built 50 miles offshore in the North Sea. This island will initially cover 120,000 sq meters and provide green energy to 3 million households. It will be protected by a high sea wall on three sides and have a dock for service vessels on the fourth side.

This project, the largest construction in Danish history, will significantly contribute to European offshore wind potential. It builds on a June agreement to create two wind energy hubs, one artificial and one on the Baltic island of Bornholm, initially supporting 5GW of wind generation and potentially expanding to 12GW.

The North Sea island may not be completed before 2033, potentially missing Denmark's 2030 target of a 70% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions from 1990 levels. However, the government aims to accelerate the process by working with private sector partners and launching discussions with windfarm developers and investors to develop a legal framework for the remaining 49% stake.

Construction is expected to start in 2026, with the next five years focused on signing private sector partners, conducting environmental impact assessments, and connecting the energy islands to Belgium, the Netherlands, and Germany. The project's success depends on these connections, as the energy produced will exceed Denmark's needs and help other countries meet their targets.

282. ID: 1850
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Mogens Lykketoft
   Statement: We must build these energy islands to help meet the Paris Agreement's 1.5C warming limit. The North Sea has the potential to generate more energy than all the oil and gas Denmark has ever produced there. Building artificial islands is the most efficient and cost-effective way to connect and distribute massive amounts of offshore wind power, not just to Denmark but to the entire European grid.

The energy islands solve multiple problems by creating a hub-and-spoke system. Instead of having scattered, individual wind farms providing small amounts of power to individual areas, these islands will serve as central collection and distribution hubs. By connecting different types of energy sources - solar, wind, hydroelectric, and nuclear - across Europe through these hubs, we can better balance the power grid without needing to store enormous amounts of wind energy.

The energy islands represent a shift from fragmented national climate policies to an integrated, transnational approach that connects multiple energy sectors. This is crucial for effectively integrating renewable energy into our power systems. However, I acknowledge that we still face significant challenges, particularly regarding energy storage solutions for these islands.

288. ID: 2605
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Irina Papazu
   Statement: Here's what I see on Samsø, and it challenges how we typically think about renewable energy transitions. The standard view of bricolage - this idea of 'making do' with whatever's available - doesn't capture what actually happened in our renewable energy project. We didn't just work with pre-existing resources or make do with scraps. Instead, my research shows we engaged in an active process of creating and transforming resources through the project itself.

The project's success required turning nearly every islander into a participant. The resources we needed - from skills to support to funding - weren't sitting there waiting to be used. We had to construct them by connecting to people's hopes and dreams, by drawing on shared cultural narratives, and by keeping the project flexible enough that people could see their own opportunities within it. This wasn't about making the best of limited resources - it was about transforming our community's latent potential into actual resources through entrepreneurial action.

What makes this particularly significant is how it remained true to Samsø's local context while fundamentally changing us from an agricultural society to a renewable energy leader. This suggests bricolage isn't a fallback strategy - it's potentially the best approach for community-based sustainability transitions where local buy-in and resource development are crucial.

This challenges both the way we think about bricolage - showing it's about resource creation, not just resource use - and how we approach community renewable energy projects. The lesson for other communities is that success doesn't depend on having all the resources up front. It's about creating the conditions where resources can emerge through the project itself.

333. ID: 1538
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Theis Palm
   Statement: My background is in political science, as I hold a master’s degree in the field. For my thesis, I chose to focus on Denmark's energy policy, particularly the interplay of interests within the energy sector. During this research, I discovered that Denmark does not actually get 50% of its energy from clean sources, as is often claimed. In reality, back then it was only about 8%, and today it’s closer to 9%. I felt compelled to highlight this fact, as it is rarely addressed in public debates.
I’ve also done some calculations regarding the energy island’s output over its lifetime. It’s expected to generate enough electricity to cover Denmark’s electricity consumption for 30 years. However, if the same amount of money were invested in building a standard nuclear power plant, we could generate enough electricity to cover our needs for 114 years. In addition, we would have free district heating to cover all our heating requirements for those same 114 years.
We often hear that this energy island will deliver 10 GW, but that’s its capacity. The wind doesn’t blow all the time, so the actual output will only be about 4.5 GW when adjusted for intermittency. For the same investment, you could instead have built 7 GW of nuclear power, which produces a steady output consistently.

341. ID: 1426
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: Earth
   Statement: Denmark is committed to building an artificial island 80 km offshore in the North Sea to serve as a clean energy hub. This island, equivalent to the size of 18 football fields, will produce and store wind energy, connecting to offshore wind turbines to supply power to 3 million households. It will also generate green hydrogen for use in shipping, aviation, and industry.

Our government has taken a majority stake in this £25 billion project. The island will have an initial capacity of 3 GW, expanding to 10 GW, and is expected to be operational by 2033. However, we acknowledge that this timeline may not align with our 2030 goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 70% from 1990 levels. The island will include high sea walls, a dock for service vessels, and will contribute to expanding Europe's offshore wind capacity.

We are also exploring a second artificial island in the Baltic Sea, with plans to increase our wind energy generation to 12 GW. This initiative aligns with the EU's goal to rely almost entirely on renewable energy within a decade. Construction will begin in 2026, and we will work with private partners and neighboring countries, including Belgium, the Netherlands, and Germany, to integrate the energy islands into a broader European network.

This project represents a significant step in Denmark's leadership in the global green transition. The energy produced will surpass Denmark's needs, allowing us to support other countries in meeting their renewable energy targets. We view this as a monumental moment for Denmark and the fight against climate change.

VRT underscores that this project, costing €600 million, is a world-first initiative and a cornerstone of a future European electricity network. It will link countries like Belgium, Denmark, and the UK, making the island not only a green energy solution but also a crucial infrastructure for international energy collaboration.

373. ID: 5594
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Hanne Lyng Winter
   Statement: The Association for Gentle Coastal Fisheries supports offshore wind energy and Denmark's goal of a 70% reduction in emissions. However, we are deeply concerned about the environmental impacts of the Energy Island projects. These projects require massive amounts of seabed material—approximately 17 million m³ for the North Sea Energy Island alone—which threatens marine ecosystems and violates EU directives on environmental preservation. Raw material extraction from the seabed already causes significant damage, destroying fish habitats and leading to biodiversity loss. Expanding raw material areas for Energy Island construction exacerbates these problems.

Gentle coastal fishing is one of the most climate-friendly sources of animal protein, as it has minimal bycatch, low energy consumption, and a negligible impact on the seabed. Energy Island construction must not destroy nature; otherwise, it cannot be considered "green energy." We advocate for the use of repurposed materials, such as those currently dumped into the sea, rather than virgin seabed resources. Furthermore, tender requirements for the Energy Islands should promote more nature conservation, gentle coastal fishing, and sustainable food production. For example, integrating facilities for cultivating seaweed and mussels around wind farm structures would align with these goals and support climate-friendly food production.

427. ID: 3047
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Hans Østergård
   Statement: The two mayors, Hans Østergård from Ringkøbing Skjern Municipality and Erik Flyvholm from Lemvig Municipality, see no reason for the establishment of the two near-shore offshore wind farms. Their reasoning is as follows:

1) Currently, Denmark has so much wind energy that many onshore wind turbines must be throttled down. The energy cannot yet be stored for use during calm periods or converted into other forms of energy.
2) The Thor offshore wind farm, with a capacity of 800-1000 MW, located about 20 km from the coast near Thorsminde, is expected to be completed by 2025/2026. Additionally, the Kriegers Flak project in the Baltic Sea, with a capacity of 600 MW, is being phased in. This will bring the total offshore wind capacity from 1700 MW in 2021 to around 2300 MW. By 2025/2026, the Thor project will increase the total to 3300 MW, almost doubling the current capacity. Therefore, the two near-shore wind farms, with a total capacity of 350 MW, are unnecessary and will only cause even more onshore turbines to stand still due to a lack of demand for electricity.
3) By 2025/2026, the mayors hope that Power-to-X technology will be developed, along with the necessary number of electric vehicle charging stations and the conversion of electricity into liquid fuel.
4) Cancelling the near-shore wind farms would save the state millions of kroner, even after compensating Vattenfall. Additionally, the fishing industries from Hvide Sande, Thorsminde, and Thyborøn would benefit from better and freer fishing conditions in the waters 0-20 km off the coast from Hvide Sande to Thyborøn.
5) The mayors are optimistic that the Energy Island in the waters off their municipalities will create many service-related jobs, and they are ready to engage in discussions to make this a win-win situation.

They look forward to hearing from Energy Minister Dan Jørgensen to arrange further discussions.

447. ID: 5597
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Simon Riis Vilhelm Verland
   Statement: Dansk Energi appreciates the opportunity to provide feedback on the proposed legislation regarding the planning and construction of an energy island in the North Sea. Dansk Energi shares the concern about potential delays due to the processing of complaints by an administrative authority. Therefore, Dansk Energi supports the notion that permits or decisions issued by the Minister for Climate, Energy, and Utilities, the Minister for the Environment, and the Minister for Culture regarding the North Sea energy island should not be subject to appeal by an administrative authority, as stated in sections 11-13 of the proposal. At the same time, Dansk Energi acknowledges the importance of ensuring that legal rights are maintained by allowing affected parties to challenge the permits and decisions in court, as outlined in section 14.

Furthermore, Dansk Energi views the proposal positively, as it would enable the Minister for Climate, Energy, and Utilities to facilitate the progress of the energy island project by acquiring necessary permits for sand extraction. Sand extraction permits are critical because the law mandates that the energy island will be a reclaimed island. The proposal allows the Minister to set rules for charging fees to cover costs related to preparing for the energy island’s construction, including processing permit applications and overseeing the project.

In this context, Dansk Energi emphasizes that the fee structure should not unnecessarily increase the cost of large-scale offshore wind development from Denmark's exclusive economic zone (EEZ). It is important that the costs associated with the preparatory work are determined before the energy island project is put out for tender, so that these costs are known when submitting bids.

The proposal does not include a time limit for the powers granted to the Minister under section 4. Therefore, Dansk Energi expresses concerns regarding potential changes to the terms for maintaining or operating the energy island after the tender process. Such changes could increase the cost of ownership for the stakeholders involved in the energy island’s ownership, especially if these terms are adjusted after the bidding process. Setting the conditions for operation and maintenance should be the responsibility of the future management board, which will be appointed by the state and private stakeholders.

Finally, the background material repeatedly mentions that the planned energy island and offshore wind farms will be located near designated Natura 2000 and marine strategy areas. Dansk Energi believes that the energy island and its associated wind farms are essential for significant societal interests, and there are no viable alternatives to the planned 10 GW energy island, based on screenings of the marine territory. The fully developed energy island could generate 40-50 TWh annually, which is significantly higher than Denmark's total electricity consumption in 2020, which was approximately 32 TWh. If there is a need to balance societal and environmental concerns, this should be considered in the decision-making process regarding potential exemptions from the nature protection laws.

To maximize the value of this endeavor, three critical actions are needed:

1. **Broader Stakeholder Engagement**: A wide-reaching discussion is essential to increase awareness and understanding of the challenges posed by energy islands and the broader decarbonization of the Danish energy system. This discussion should focus on the societal impact and use energy islands as tangible examples of the green transition. Training programs should also target company employees and those transitioning into the green sector.

3. **Advancing Denmark’s Green Leadership and Export Potential**: Offshore energy islands reaffirm Denmark’s leadership in green energy. They allow Denmark to guide the development of offshore wind while helping other countries leapfrog technological stages. The lessons learned from building and operating these “electron metropolises” will attract international interest and strengthen Denmark’s competitiveness and export potential. While energy systems are not direct export products, their components and associated services are.

Energy islands provide unparalleled opportunities for businesses to innovate, for policymakers and regulators to develop necessary frameworks, and for universities to create solutions and train professionals. Sharing this knowledge will advance the global green transition.

457. ID: 241
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Technical University of Denmark, Aalborg University
   Statement: How to integrate offshore energy islands into the Danish energy system
The energy produced on the islands, either in the form of electricity or other forms of energy, will be traded on the markets. Experience from previous projects in Denmark in connection with integrated energy systems shows that it is crucial to develop well-functioning coordination mechanisms between the energy markets, including a market for electricity and hydrogen. Without these mechanisms, the energy system will not be able to fully exploit the existing flexibility in other energy sectors, in particular the flexibility in power-to-gas assets.
It is important to develop appropriate “market-based” coordination mechanisms between the energy sectors (electricity, heating, gas/hydrogen). This can be achieved by defining new market products and/or introducing new market actors at the interface of the energy systems and/or by defining new bidding formats.
Furthermore, the physics of the integrated energy system, including the power-to-gas assets, must be correctly represented in the market clearing problem, which must at the same time be kept mathematically simple enough to derive efficient
prices.
The two energy islands will become the largest concentration of production units in the Danish energy system.
Combined with the inherent variability in their wind power production, they will challenge the balance between supply and demand in the Danish energy system.
The energy system's current mechanisms for redundancy and security of supply in the event of a malfunction in the largest units cannot handle units of the size represented by the energy islands.
Although part of the challenge can be solved by incorporating redundancy into the design of the electrical infrastructure, it is likely that these mechanisms will need to be reconsidered and adapted.
The abundance of cheap, green electricity production from, among others, offshore wind makes electrification the natural next step towards decarbonized energy systems. But electrification alone will not be enough. That is why hydrogen is currently being considered as a future cornerstone of a fully integrated energy system that combines renewable electricity with green fuels for sectors such as heavy-duty road transport, aviation, shipping and the steel industry.
The production of green fuels can become an integral part of energy islands.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

458. ID: 240
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Technical University of Denmark, Aalborg University
   Statement: How to expand offshore energy islands
Preparations for the energy islands are in full swing, with the aim of establishing operations by 2033 at the latest. However, once they are built, they will exist for a much longer time and be able to handle significantly larger electricity production based on offshore wind and possibly also the electricity consumption in power-to-gas plants. The energy island in the North Sea will be built for 3 GW, but must
be designed to be expandable to 10 GW and potentially be connected to other islands to form a
European offshore DC grid.
The energy islands therefore represent a significant change in the paradigm of how offshore connections have been built so far. Today, offshore connections are built between individual production units (a
wind farm or an oil/gas platform) and an entry point to the energy system. There is no experience
with reinforcing or modifying offshore connections for expansion once they are in operation.
The scale of this challenge becomes clear when you look at how quickly technology is developing in areas such as power electronics. The initial design must be scalable, i.e. able to be expanded with more devices with their own control, without the need for extensive retrofitting or major design changes. At all stages, the technology chosen must allow for a high degree of freedom and not limit future expansion with more intelligent solutions, while ensuring a high degree of robustness. Another critical challenge is ensuring that system components can “talk” to each other and work together. This is called interoperability*. There will be a significant number of power electronic devices on
offshore energy islands – either as inverters in wind turbines or as large HVDC converters. Power electronic converters are versatile and flexible devices with complex and advanced control algorithms. Operationally, converters are (almost) exclusively defined by their control (software) rather than by their physical characteristics (hardware), which primarily define the converters’ limitations. In their final form, the offshore energy islands’ electrical system will include multiple wind farms and HVDC converters from multiple manufacturers, and their control systems will be specific and proprietary to each supplier.
Therefore, a system (wind farm) or a component (HVDC converter) must be able to work effectively with other systems and/or components from another supplier. The challenge here is to develop a process that ensures interoperability without requiring full disclosure of the detailed converter control from the manufacturers. And this must be done knowing that the converter control software (and hardware technology) of 2030 will likely be significantly different from what is available today.

480. ID: 2109
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Society for Nature Conservation
   Statement: We are deeply concerned about the impact of the Bornholm Energy Island construction on the critically endangered Baltic Sea porpoise population. The specific area designated for offshore wind turbines serves as winter habitat for these porpoises. The total population consists of only 500 individuals, with fewer than 100 being breeding females. According to an ICES report, the loss of even one individual per year from human activities like bycatch could have devastating effects on the entire population. Since Baltic Sea porpoises are protected under Annex IV, Denmark has a legal obligation to protect these marine mammals wherever they are found.

The environmental impact assessment for Bornholm Energy Island must thoroughly address and detail specific measures to protect the porpoise population from underwater noise pollution, both during the construction phase and the operational phase of the wind turbines.

To ensure clarity, unnecessary references that could be interpreted as prescriptive have been removed from the text.

The ministry confirms that the parameters for the island’s size and the use of an innovation zone will not be finalized in the legislation itself but rather in the tender materials authorized by the legislation. Following the September 1, 2021, preparatory agreement by the political coalition supporting the climate agreement, bidders will be allowed to propose additional areas on the island for commercial and innovative purposes within the ownership model framework. This approach is intended to leverage the commercial, industrial, and technical expertise of the market and to ensure the potential activation of economies of scale during the construction phase.

Furthermore, since the legislation includes provisions for granting construction permits, it was necessary to describe the scope of these powers. However, adjustments have been made to the legislative text to remove unnecessary details that could be seen as overly directive.

495. ID: 879
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: Financial viability and (un)profitability
   Actor: Private person
   Statement: Here are my concerns about the Energy Island projects, though much remains unknown:

1. The plan to install 12 GW of additional wind turbines to supply electricity to neighboring countries is fundamentally flawed. Neighboring countries also have surpluses of wind-generated electricity at the same time as Denmark, which means we will often struggle to export this electricity. This issue already exists today.

2. Wind turbines only generate electricity when the wind blows. For approximately 40-60 days per year, other energy sources will need to cover the electricity demand. Current information does not explain where this electricity will come from during calm weather.

3. A portion of the surplus electricity is intended for Power-to-X (PtX) production, such as fuel for aviation. PtX requires both hydrogen (H) and carbon (C). Hydrogen can come from wind-powered electricity, but the source of carbon is unclear. Will it come from CO2 captured at power plants in Zealand or Jutland—plants that political parties simultaneously demand to shut down? The other Energy Island will presumably also require CO2 from Zealand.

4. In addition to the estimated costs of 38 billion kroner and 210 billion kroner for the Energy Island projects, further investments will be needed for wind turbines, PtX facilities, pipelines, and long underwater power cables. This could add another 100 billion kroner, though the exact amount is unknown.

5. Assuming these cost estimates are accurate, the total expense would be around 300 billion kroner, which equates to 50,000 kroner per Dane, including infants, or 200,000 kroner per average household.

6. Although some of the investment is expected to come from private funds, this does not change the fact that the projects place a significant financial burden on society. This money could be used for initiatives with more certain benefits.

7. The costs of wind power, along with the additional required investments, are now so high that Denmark could instead build 4-5 nuclear power plants. These nuclear plants would provide reliable electricity regardless of wind conditions, without the need for energy islands. They would meet all Danish and EU climate requirements for the next 50-60 years, whereas offshore wind turbines typically last only 20-25 years.

I suspect that most members of Parliament who approved these projects have very little understanding of these issues. Even Dan Jørgensen dismissed the idea of nuclear power in Berlingske last year as 'completely unrealistic,' despite its clear advantages over the Energy Island plan.

508. ID: 821
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Alessandro Singlitico, Jacob Østergaard, Spyros Chatzivasileiadis
   Statement: We believe the Danish Energy Islands' offshore hydrogen production needs significant development before implementation at gigawatt scale. Our current cost estimates for hydrogen infrastructure are based on discussions with industry players, not proven deployments. We've simplified our analysis to focus only on major system components, as this will help guide more detailed future studies.
While our economic analysis offers a starting point, we see three key opportunities to reduce offshore green hydrogen costs:
1. We should leverage existing North Sea oil and gas infrastructure by converting current platforms and pipelines for hydrogen use. 
2. We need to integrate hydrogen and electrical transmission systems into unified components rather than building separate infrastructure. This would cut installation costs and allow hydrogen facilities to provide grid balancing services.
3. We must create synergies with industrial systems by utilizing electrolysis byproducts like oxygen and heat, and by exploring conversion into e-fuels.
We acknowledge that our analysis excludes social and environmental impacts, which are crucial factors in determining optimal facility placement.

513. ID: 2680
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Climate, Energy and Utilities Committee
   Statement: The Danish Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities has proposed a law to authorize the planning, design, and construction of the Energy Island in the North Sea. This legislation defines the scope of activities necessary to develop the Energy Island while delineating responsibilities and regulatory frameworks.

Key provisions of the law include:

1. The Energy Island will be a reclaimed island located in Denmark's exclusive economic zone off the west coast of Jutland.
2. The legislation does not cover power generation facilities, electrical transmission networks, or international interconnectors connected to the Energy Island.
3. The Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities will be responsible for preparing and conducting the tender process, granting construction permits, and overseeing the project.
4. Construction permits will specify the island’s design, size, and structure, based on project descriptions and applications from project applicants. The Ministry may impose conditions on construction, maintenance, and operational activities.
5. The Ministry will manage all environmental assessments and approvals under Danish environmental law, and these approvals will replace the need for additional environmental decisions under related legislation.
6. The law includes provisions to ensure public accessibility to information about permits and decisions.
7. The Ministry will oversee compliance with the law and may impose fines or penalties for violations, such as unauthorized construction or failure to meet permit conditions.
8. Appeals regarding permits or decisions under the law are not allowed, with judicial review limited to six months after publication or notification of the decision.
9. Provisions are included for setting fees to cover costs associated with project preparation, permitting, and oversight.

The law is designed to streamline the regulatory and administrative processes, ensuring efficient development of the Energy Island while maintaining compliance with environmental and international obligations. The legislation takes effect on January 1, 2022.

514. ID: 2692
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: DN og World Wildlife Fond
   Statement: The Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities acknowledges the comment raised by DN (The Danish Society for Nature Conservation) and WWF regarding the omission of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 14, which pertains to life below water, in the section assessing the impacts on the fulfillment of the United Nations’ SDGs. The Ministry has noted this comment and has since incorporated an evaluation of the proposed bill’s consequences on SDG 14. While several of its targets are not relevant because they concern the year 2020, it is recommended to highlight target 14.c. This target aims to increase the protection and sustainable use of oceans and their resources by implementing international laws reflected in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. 

Regarding the potential environmental impacts of constructing an enclosed island in the North Sea, these impacts are not well understood. However, as described in section 9 of the bill, which addresses environmental and natural consequences, the project could have both positive and negative environmental effects. The Ministry explains how potential environmental impacts will be assessed as part of the environmental review of the energy island plan (SMV) and the environmental impact assessment (VVM) for the specific project. These environmental assessments are designed to minimize impacts through careful planning, which will also be conducted in coordination with other authorities involved in ocean use, as part of the maritime spatial planning process. Overall, the Ministry expects that the bill will primarily have a positive effect on the SDGs.

Eventually, the capacity will increase to ten gigawatts, powering ten million households. The island will also support Power-to-X technology to convert offshore wind power into fuels for ships, planes, and trucks. The island, when fully built, will cover an area equivalent to 64 football fields.

Despite criticism from Ørsted, which raised concerns about the cost, inflexibility, and feasibility of producing hydrogen on the island, the project will proceed as planned. The state will retain majority ownership to ensure the infrastructure remains under national control, making this the largest public-private partnership in Denmark’s history. The investor consortium Vindø, which includes PensionDanmark and Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, has shown interest in the project.

This Energy Island is a cornerstone of Denmark’s 70% CO2 reduction goal by 2030 and represents a key initiative to position Denmark as a global leader in renewable energy. The North Sea project follows a separate agreement to establish a two-gigawatt Energy Island in the Baltic Sea, where Bornholm will serve as the hub for offshore wind power.

Three primary sources of risk for the Bornholm Energy Island’s electrical infrastructure project are:

579. ID: 2337

By transitioning to green electricity, we can significantly reduce our dependence on fossil fuels, including Russian oil, coal, and gas.

The energy islands, which include artificial islands (such as Denmark’s energy island in the North Sea) and technical facilities on existing islands (like the energy island planned for Bornholm), represent a breakthrough in energy infrastructure. These islands will connect surrounding offshore wind farms to the electricity grids of multiple countries, enabling the distribution of green electricity directly to households and businesses across borders.

We are convinced that energy islands will enable the production of green electricity on an unprecedented scale. This innovation will help phase out fossil fuel-based energy production and pave the way for a more sustainable energy future. To ensure a reliable energy supply, even in a renewable-energy-driven system dependent on weather conditions, it is critical to fully harness the potential of the North Sea. Establishing a robust cross-border energy infrastructure will optimize our wind resources, and energy islands will play a central role in achieving this goal.

Moreover, energy islands will empower Europe to electrify large segments of society while making electricity consumption greener for households and businesses alike. These islands also have immense potential to serve as hubs for energy storage and for converting green electricity into sustainable fuels through Power-to-X technologies. This will provide solutions for heavy transportation sectors, such as aviation and shipping, further advancing our green transition.

We are committed to supporting these developments and ensuring that energy islands become a cornerstone of Europe’s sustainable energy future.

604. ID: 4845
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Claus Møller
   Statement: The enthusiasm surrounding Power-to-X (PtX) and its role in the green transition is evident, with numerous seminars and large-scale plans being discussed across Europe. The EU is even offering significant financial incentives, including €750 billion in COVID-recovery funds, to support PtX plants and hydrogen infrastructure like pipelines and storage.  

However, the conversation often overlooks the poor efficiency of the conversion from electricity to hydrogen, which, with current technologies, struggles to exceed 50%. One suggested solution is to use the excess heat for district heating, but this raises serious practical concerns.  

Take Esbjerg as an example. When the Esbjerg plant—a 378 MW facility that supplied electricity and heat—closes in 2023, its heating will be replaced with a combination of a 50 MW seawater heat pump, a 60 MW biomass plant, and a 30 MW electric boiler. Yet, plans for energy conversion in Esbjerg include:  

- Høst PtX Esbjerg with 1 GW capacity  
- H2 Energy with 1 GW capacity  
- A fully built-out hydrogen factory at 12 MW  
- Various pyrolysis plants exceeding 10 MW  

All these projects claim their waste heat can be used for district heating, but the combined output would be around 20 times the actual heating demand in Esbjerg. This mismatch highlights the inefficiency and lack of foresight in these plans.  

On a broader scale, the same inefficiency exists for energy islands in the North and Baltic Seas. Performing energy conversion at sea, where there is no need for district heating, exacerbates the issue of waste. While some envision humans colonizing Mars or the Moon, perhaps it would be more practical and cost-effective to build artificial islands in the North Sea to utilize this excess heat. Yet, even this is unlikely to be part of current plans.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The offshore wind farms will be established approximately 15 km south-southwest of the coast and will be visible to the naked eye, but not dominate the horizon. Bornholm´s Airport is Denmark´s only state-owned airport administered by Trafikstyrelsen and operated by a local management team. The airport is as mentioned above located in the South Western corner of Bornholm with the coordinates 55°03′48″N 014°45′34″Ø close to Rønne town and to the sea in the western direction of the new windfarms. 
The airport has a 2002 m long and 45 m wide runway and service all kinds of aviation comprising: Scheduled passenger traffic mainly to Copenhagen, Charter traffic, Cargo traffic, General Aviation traffic (GA traffic), Search and Rescue traffic (SAR traffic), Military surveillance traffic. 
The airport is counted among the smaller airports in Denmark and had in 2021 180.000 arriving and departing passengers heavily influenced by the Corona pandemic. 
The location of Bornholm 1 and 2 will not interfere with the outer horizon for the instrument approach and landings with a 15 km distance between the windfarm and the airport. However, if the northern tip of the windfarm is moved closer to the airport to allow for more wind from the sea it may be necessary to move the upper rows of windmills to another location in the windfarm areas to avoid a conflict with the 15 km outer surface. The above-mentioned analysis of aviation related issues and scope of work will comprise civil traffic, military traffic, helicopter traffic and drone traffic.
