617. ID: 5545
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Dan Jørgensen
   Statement: I have approved Energinet's application for the "Energiø Bornholm Electrical Infrastructure" project. This project aims to establish the necessary collective transmission network and associated electrical facilities to connect the Energy Island of Bornholm to Denmark's electricity transmission grid. Specifically, it includes a 245 km direct current connection between Bornholm and Zealand and the construction of two 400 kV stations with converter facilities on Bornholm and Zealand.

The approval follows thorough technical reviews and political agreements, including the expansion of Energiø Bornholm's capacity from 2 GW to 3 GW as of the August 2022 political supplementary agreement, and a July 2022 agreement with Germany for their connection to the Energy Island via the German TSO, 50Hertz. Negotiations on the allocation of ownership, costs, and revenues between Energinet and 50Hertz are ongoing.

As per preliminary assessments, the project's construction budget for Energinet has been reduced from DKK 16.9 billion to approximately DKK 13.9 billion, excluding risk costs, due to co-financing principles established in the agreement with Germany. Operating costs have similarly been projected to decrease from DKK 121 million to DKK 114 million annually.

The project must be executed as outlined in the submitted materials, adhering to the specified technical solutions and assumptions within Energinet’s business case. Any significant changes to the project must be promptly reported to the Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities for separate approval.

630. ID: 5749
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: German collaboration
   Actor: Paul E. Seifert
   Statement: We find that cost reductions and offshore wind development plans can help decarbonize Europe’s energy system, though expanded capacity increases grid congestion. We identify Power-to-Gas technology as a flexible solution to ease these issues, with hydrogen reducing emissions in hard-to-decarbonize sectors. Using an integrated model, we analyze the Bornholm Energy Island, combining offshore wind, Power-to-Gas, and inter-country electricity connections. Our findings confirm that large wind hubs cause congestion and curtailment, but we show that optimal investments in electricity lines and electrolysers can mitigate these effects. While current costs favor increasing electricity lines over electrolyser deployment, a higher hydrogen market price could make electrolysers more viable. We conclude that inter-country connections, especially to Poland or Sweden, provide the most value, with Denmark offering the least benefits contrary to initial plans.

632. ID: 5714
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Ken'ichi Matsumoto ,  Yuko Matsumura
   Statement: We, Ken'ichi Matsumoto and Yuko Matsumura, believe that promoting renewable energy (RE) electricity in remote islands is critical due to its potential to address climate change and reduce reliance on expensive and less sustainable thermal power generation. Based on our research in Tsushima, we identified the key barriers to RE development as insufficient investment in infrastructure, such as grid capacity, and the lack of local technical expertise to maintain RE facilities. To overcome these barriers, we advocate for urgent investments in grid enhancements and the cultivation of local experts.

Our analysis reveals that promoting RE, including photovoltaic (PV) and wind power, generates economic benefits such as local employment (4.21–19.30 jobs annually within the island) and additional revenue for both the island (JPY 101.14–461.45 million/year) and external regions (JPY 212.60–977.32 million/year). While the local economic impacts may appear modest, these benefits contribute to regional development and can facilitate public acceptance of RE projects.

We recognize that conflicts between local residents and RE developers could arise during project acceleration, particularly due to potential environmental concerns like impacts on landscapes and ecosystems. To address this, we emphasize the need for proactive dialogue with residents to build consensus and implement precautionary measures.

Additionally, remote islands without mainland grid connections require investments in energy storage systems to stabilize the variable capacities of PV and wind power. Given the high costs of thermal power plants and the fact that part of the energy costs for these islands is subsidized by citizens elsewhere, RE adoption is not only more sustainable but also economically advantageous for both local and external communities. Future research should explore the socioeconomic impacts of expanded RE penetration alongside energy storage systems to further inform these initiatives.

The enormous onshore facility will span nearly 100 hectares (around 150 football fields) and possibly even more if additional offshore wind turbines are built near Bornholm, which is very likely. This causes a drastic drop in property values for us as neighbors. Properties and homes located close to the facility become impossible to sell at a normal price. If these properties are sold, it will be at a fraction of their value before the energy island project and its location were announced.
We estimate that properties up to three kilometers from the facility will lose significant value.
We urge everyone on Bornholm, including the politicians here, to find another location on the island to build the PTX plant. The whole of Bornholm must help carry the energy island, not just us living south of Aakirkeby.
The energy island projects are part of the green transition to save the climate. The war in Ukraine has created an energy crisis, making the green transition even more urgent. We can expect these projects to be implemented with maximum speed and minimal room to avoid errors.
It appears that the energy island projects will move forward quickly and have broad support among the public and in Parliament. We live in a democracy, and when it has been decided that the energy island projects are to be realized, we must accept it—even if we live in the area and become neighbors to the facility, which will be built on land expropriated by the state.
However, we, as neighbors to the upcoming facility, cannot accept losing a significant part of our property value. Since the location of the facility was announced, we have been unable to sell homes in the area. Potential buyers are waiting until the facility is built before purchasing, which means the problem will persist for many years.
When the Danish people—and therefore the state—have initiated the energy island projects, the majority of the population is responsible for causing a significant economic loss for the small minority of us who live near the facility. We cannot accept this!
When the majority in Denmark has decided that Energy Island Bornholm should be realized, the same majority must help cover the costs so that the energy island and other energy projects do not ruin those of us who are unfortunate enough to become neighbors to the facility. There are enough disadvantages beyond the economic ones!
We demand the creation of laws ensuring that neighbors to such facilities are compensated. This could be achieved by expanding the compensation scheme to include large transformer stations and cable facilities, which can easily be compared to solar panel and wind turbine installations that are already covered. These legislative changes must apply retroactively from when the Energy Island Bornholm project was announced.
The state will earn money by selling green electricity abroad over the next 50 years, and the rest of Denmark will benefit from green power from Energy Island Bornholm. But if we, as neighbors to the facility, are not compensated, we will do everything we can to oppose Energy Island Bornholm.
If every citizen in Denmark experienced a 50% reduction in property value due to the green transition, I doubt there would be much support for it. Imagine that scenario!
We have repeatedly heard from Energinet and Bornholm’s Regional Municipality that they value dialogue and are eager to listen to us. Well, it’s time for them to start that dialogue. Dialogue means an exchange of viewpoints, especially between conflicting parties, to reach mutual agreement—unlike a unilateral imposition.
We have submitted a citizens’ proposal to Parliament and urge all politicians to take it seriously and do the necessary work to change the law.
We are more than willing to contribute to the work if someone is willing to listen!
If Denmark wants to avoid even greater resistance to the green transition, our politicians need to take us seriously—not just listen but act. And they need to act now!

661. ID: 551
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: Bring out the champagne! Denmark is set to gain a new island—the world's first energy island—located 80 kilometers offshore in the North Sea. 

This energy island will be an artificial structure designed to collect and distribute electricity generated by surrounding offshore wind farms. Initially, the island will have a capacity of 3 gigawatts, enough to power 3 million European households. Over time, the capacity will be expanded to 10 gigawatts, sufficient to supply 10 million households.

While the exact design is still being finalized, the island capable of handling 3 gigawatts of offshore wind is expected to span at least 120,000 square meters, equivalent to 18 football fields. Once expanded to handle 10 gigawatts, the island's size could increase to an area comparable to 64 football fields.

With the completion of the first phase of the energy islands, Denmark’s offshore wind capacity will nearly quadruple. When fully developed, the energy islands will bring Denmark’s capacity to seven times the current level.

We aim for a cost-efficient buildout of offshore wind that will harvest the potential of the North Sea in the most beneficial way for both the connected countries and the European Union overall.
Together, we have set ambitious combined targets for offshore wind of at least 65 GW by 2030. Based on the North Sea as a Green Power Plant of Europe, together we aim to more than double our total capacity of offshore wind to at least 150 GW by 2050, delivering more than half of capacity needed to reach EU climate neutrality according to the European Commission’s Strategy on Offshore Renewable Energy. This will contribute to large-scale onshore and offshore production of green hydrogen. We have set combined targets of about 20 GW production capacity already by 2030 and look to expand our production even further for 2050.

For Bornholm, one idea could be offering boat trips to the offshore wind turbines, allowing visitors to get a close-up view. Similar to Læsø, where a spa uses salt from the island’s saltworks, Bornholm could develop hot springs powered by renewable energy, offering either wellness or health benefits to visitors.

695. ID: 832
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Erik Damsgaard Christensen
   Statement: My reeserch showes that having substations on separate platforms in the North Sea instead of concentrating everything on the main Energy Island would be a smart engineering choice. The platforms can effectively house the equipment needed to convert power from the wind turbines to direct current, which is better for long-distance transmission due to lower power loss. We know from decades of oil and gas industry experience how to build platforms at the right height to withstand North Sea conditions and waves. This approach would also reduce the size requirements for the main artificial island. With the large number of turbines planned and the extensive cabling network needed, it makes practical sense to have these satellite substations closer to the turbine clusters. Building and securing such platforms on the open sea is entirely feasible from an engineering perspective - we've done this kind of thing before with oil and gas infrastructure. While research continues, putting substations on platforms is a well-established practice. The final configuration will depend on whoever wins the tender, but this distributed platform approach could be a very effective way to optimize the overall energy island concept.

697. ID: 803
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Elisabetta M. Venco
   Statement: I, Elisabetta M. Venco from the University of Pavia, believe that Energy Communities are crucial for Europe's energy transition. These communities, where citizens actively participate in renewable energy projects, offer a more democratic and inclusive approach to energy systems. 

While renewable energy production and distributed consumption are distinct concepts, they can overlap, as seen in the "renewable islands" concept. Importantly, these communities are not just about renewable energy; they can involve various activities like energy efficiency, storage, and grid management. 

The EU's legal framework for Citizen Energy Communities (CEC) and Renewable Energy Communities (REC) has paved the way for their growth. These communities can significantly contribute to the energy market by: 

* Revitalizing local economies 
* Creating jobs 
* Increasing renewable energy investments 
* Optimizing the energy system 
* Decarbonizing Europe 

Citizen participation in these communities is driven by various factors, including economic, environmental, social, and political motivations. 
In the context of urban development, Energy Communities are vital for achieving sustainable energy solutions. They enhance citizen acceptance of renewable energy projects, attract private investment, and provide direct benefits to people, such as lower electricity bills. 

Europe's energy market is undergoing a fundamental transformation, moving towards a distributed model with active citizen participation. I believe that citizens are the cornerstone of this energy transition, and their involvement is essential for its success.

713. ID: 2714
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Bent Kiertzner
   Statement: Mr. Bertel Maigaard, Biocirc must surely have been inspired by the young and ambitious engineer Sidenius in Henrik Pontoppidan’s masterpiece Lykke-Per. Jutland needs to be modernized in terms of energy, and while Biocirc’s methods are now more modern than those proposed by Sidenius in the book, they are just as grandiose.

I hope politicians, civil servants, and project developers read the book. There is much inspiration to be drawn from it.

Tjele Langsø could be equipped with a giant hose connected to a large heat pump, which could provide free heat to the entire surrounding area. Before that, the phosphorus- and nitrogen-rich sludge covering the lakebed—currently suffocating the lake—could be removed and sent as free fertilizer to the Horn of Africa to help combat famine there. The geese that Ulrik Wilbek is eager to see disappear could, in their deceased state, be used in biogas plants, and once the geese are gone, perhaps swans and eagles killed by wind turbine blades could replace them.

The entire population of trash fish in the lake should be fished out to improve water quality, and these fish could also be used in biogas production. This would provide employment for fishermen who have lost their livelihoods due to the oxygen depletion in Danish waters and the consequent collapse of fish stocks. And so, we could continue.

The only requirement, as with Engineer Sidenius, is to disregard trivial banalities such as economic feasibility and environmental considerations. Then everything will run smoothly.

Apart from wind turbines, biogas, and solar panels, all the other elements of the so-called energy island are still undeveloped. Nonetheless, the economics of the project are claimed to be completely under control. There might be a few hundred million kroner for the citizens of Viborg and nearly free heating, and hopefully, a little will also go to Lykke-Per. Now, that’s quite certain.

Historically, in 2012, a favorable scheme was introduced, allowing private individuals to install solar panels on their homes and produce more electricity than they consumed. The surplus electricity could be deposited into the grid and retrieved when the solar panels were not producing enough.

The scheme was politically guaranteed to last at least 20 years, and solar panels were installed everywhere. They were installed where electricity was primarily consumed, which was entirely logical. Several municipalities sensibly wanted to install solar panels on their public buildings, but such anarchy could not be tolerated, and the state began losing revenue from energy taxes.

Municipalities were then required to create a separate company for each installation, which was obviously unmanageable. With the stroke of a pen, the scheme was rendered impossible. It was simply too favorable for private individuals.

Solar panels were installed everywhere, and citizens felt engaged in the green transition. But this could not be allowed to continue, so the scheme was quickly tightened and made less favorable. People stopped installing solar panels on a large scale. All that remained was the 20-year guarantee given to the first naïve individuals who believed in the state and political promises.

The then Minister for Energy, Supply, and Climate, Lars Chr. Lilleholt of the Liberal Party, was tasked with addressing this and solved it perfectly. The guarantee was abolished, effective January 1, 2020. That was the end of that. Let that be a lesson. Never trust a used car dealer or a politician.

Now solar panel owners receive about half the price for their surplus production compared to what they pay for electricity from their supplier. At times, like in the spring of 2021, it even cost private solar panel owners money to deliver electricity to the grid. You simply cannot have production where consumption also occurs—it’s pure anarchy.

What do we do, then? Since we cannot have self-sufficient electricity production in cities or factories where the electricity is immediately consumed, we must move to the countryside. This can solve several problems. A new scheme was introduced, allowing large-scale solar panel installations on agricultural land.

A skilled farmer can earn 6,000–7,000 kroner per hectare through food production. Remember—never trust a used car dealer or a politician, but this certainly does not apply to Liberal Party politicians when large agricultural interests need to be served.

It had to be done, and done effectively. A 20–30% advantage over traditional agricultural production wasn’t enough, so the scheme was designed so that by installing solar panels on good agricultural land, the landowner earns a net return of 15,000 kroner per hectare per year, without doing anything.

Now that’s something that works. Naturally, enterprising farmers are now lining up to install solar panels on their fields. You can’t blame them; it’s a win-win situation because:

Enterprising farmers are freed from the hassle of producing food and instead receive generous rewards. That’s good Liberal Party policy.
Much valuable farmland is removed from production. Reportedly, Denmark, after Bangladesh, is the most cultivated country in the world. This quickly rectifies that.
Nitrogen emissions into surrounding waters are significantly reduced.
Finally, electricity is produced in most places where it cannot be consumed locally, but an Engineer Sidenius solution can be found for that later. Always remember—ignore trivial banalities such as economic feasibility and environmental considerations. Problems are meant to be solved.
Attentive readers may already have noticed that Danish wind turbines often stand idle under favorable wind conditions. This happens because Danish wind turbines are already shut down up to 10% of the time due to what the wind industry calls "special regulation."

It’s simply impossible to utilize the electricity produced. However, here, too, a brilliant solution has been found. The Germans control and shut down Danish wind turbines—it’s not allowed in Germany—and simultaneously pay Danish wind turbine owners full compensation for lost production. That’s genius. A true Engineer Sidenius solution.

And so, everyone in the area became happy—the landowners, the mayor, and perhaps even Lykke-Per a bit more—but that was certainly well-deserved.

This project is operated by Energinet and German grid operator 50Hertz, of which Elia owns 80%. Hybrid projects combine generation and transmission elements and connect two or more markets, unlike traditional offshore wind farms that send power to shore via individual cables to a single country.

The big problem is that all parties must have the incentive to join the development of hybrid projects, and that is not currently the case. Current regulation does not allow for the necessary sharing of costs and revenue that would incentivize all parties to invest. Despite this, Ørsted, which has built roughly a quarter of the world's wind farms at sea, sees hybrid projects as crucial to unlocking offshore wind's future potential. We think that hybrids can be a huge saving of time, money, and hassle.

For this reason, the Danish Energy Agency expects only a 20% increase in onshore wind turbines over the next eight years, according to a response to the Climate Committee in Parliament.

Concerns for nature also often clash with plans for more onshore wind turbines. In North Jutland, Denmark's largest onshore wind farm at Thorup-Sletten was delayed because, according to critics, the turbines posed a threat to several animal species, including the birds of prey, the marsh harrier and the hen harrier.

I believe the state should play a bigger role and ensure that more municipalities participate in building wind turbines.

749. ID: 4795
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: The Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: Cheers to this milestone! 🍾🥂

Denmark is about to gain an additional island—the world’s first energy island, to be established 80 km off the coast in the North Sea.

The energy island will be constructed as an artificial island designed to collect and distribute electricity from surrounding offshore wind farms. Initially, the island will have a capacity of 3 GW, enough to power 3 million European households. Over time, the capacity will be expanded to 10 GW 😵

While the exact design is still being finalized, the island, capable of handling 3 gigawatts of offshore wind power, is expected to cover at least 120,000 m², which is equivalent to 18 football fields 🤘

Eventually, the capacity will be increased from 3 to 10 gigawatts, enough to power 10 million households. When expanded, the island is expected to occupy a minimum area equivalent to 64 football fields.

Upon completion of the first phase, Denmark’s offshore wind capacity will be nearly four times larger than it is today. By the time the energy islands are fully built, the installed capacity will be seven times greater than our current capacity 💪

The farmland in this area, one of the best on Bornholm, is also rich in iron oxide, which has previously caused pollution in the protected Risebæk river. Past drainage and excavation activities have contaminated the river with iron oxide, turning the water red/orange and periodically destroying all aquatic life. This pollution extends all the way to the river's outlet in the Baltic Sea, known as the "red waterfall."

765. ID: 255
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities
   Statement: We, the Danish Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities, assert that the profitability of the energy islands is a fundamental requirement, as established in the 2020 Climate Agreement for Energy and Industry. However, we recognize that the economic viability of the Energy Island at Bornholm remains highly uncertain, relying heavily on assumptions about the future development of renewable energy capacity, broader energy systems, and electricity demand both domestically and internationally beyond 2030.

We emphasize that profitability can only be demonstrated under specific scenarios, and even then, it is subject to significant uncertainty. We cannot guarantee that the project will be profitable or free from the need for subsidies. To support decision-making, we have conducted two analyses: a traditional cost-benefit analysis evaluating the societal economic viability of the project as a whole and a supplementary analysis examining the island's cost-effectiveness as infrastructure for consolidating offshore wind energy and facilitating electricity distribution between Denmark and Germany.

In scenarios based on frozen policy assumptions, we find substantial economic deficits for both societal and project finances. However, scenarios that account for partial alignment with renewable energy and electricity demand goals indicate the potential for profitability. These scenarios include contributions from Germany toward transmission costs and anticipated EU financing, which could enable the project to achieve breakeven in societal economic terms.

That said, we acknowledge that the project faces challenges stemming from global volatility in raw material prices and geopolitical uncertainties, such as the ongoing conflict in Ukraine. These factors introduce additional uncertainties regarding the final costs and economic outcomes of the project.

772. ID: 2759
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Private person
   Statement: The Danish state's planned energy islands are a necessary step for green transition, but the location proposed by Viborg Municipality is completely unacceptable. Viborg Municipality has suggested placing one of these massive industrial facilities near the south side of Lake Tjele (Tjele Langsø), in an area that was recently ruled illegal for just 8 wind turbines after extensive review by state authorities.

This area represents our most valuable, vulnerable, and internationally protected natural habitat. The taiga geese at Lake Tjele are indicator species for this habitat's exceptional biodiversity, just as black grouse once were for Jutland's heaths before those disappeared. These geese require this specific location for winter survival - they need to feed during daylight hours and safely roost on the lake at night, arriving in noisy flocks after dark. The geese are site-loyal and cannot simply relocate elsewhere.

Viborg Municipality's leadership falsely frames this as a choice between "four dead geese" versus people losing their homes. This grossly misrepresents the issue - it's about maintaining a viable population of an internationally protected migratory species for which Denmark has specific treaty obligations. The municipality is even trying to exclude consideration of these international agreements in their environmental impact assessment by claiming they aren't implemented in Danish law.

As a resident by Lake Tjele, I naturally care about protecting this environment. It's deeply concerning that local politicians criticize citizens for gathering knowledge and participating in democratic debate about our natural surroundings. This criticism of civic engagement represents a threat to democracy itself.'

775. ID: 162
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Climate, Energy and Utilities Committee
   Statement: I have approved Energinet’s application for the "Energy Island Bornholm electrical infrastructure" project. The project involves establishing a 245 km direct current connection between Bornholm and Zealand, along with two 400 kV stations with converter facilities on Bornholm and Zealand. This infrastructure will connect Energy Island Bornholm to Denmark's electricity transmission grid.  

Following a political supplementary agreement on August 29, 2022, the Energy Island Bornholm project has been expanded from 2 GW to 3 GW. Additionally, a political agreement with Germany was reached on July 26, 2022, enabling Germany to connect to Energy Island Bornholm. Energinet has preliminarily assessed that this agreement will reduce the project’s budget due to cost-sharing with the German TSO, 50Hertz. As a result, Energinet’s construction budget has been reduced from 16.9 billion DKK to approximately 13.9 billion DKK, excluding risk costs. Similarly, annual operating costs have been reduced from 121 million DKK to 114 million DKK.  

Energinet’s application has been reviewed based on the submitted materials, including the technical solutions and assumptions outlined in the business case. The project must proceed in accordance with these specifications. Any significant changes to the project must be promptly reported to the Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities for separate approval.

786. ID: 146
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: Assessment and Expected Decision

The Danish Energy Agency has assessed that the project is necessary. It is determined that the 1.2 GW connection from Zealand to Bornholm can accommodate the need for integrating renewable energy (RE) from 3 GW of offshore wind power near Bornholm, in conjunction with the international connection to Germany, which is set at 2 GW. The international connection to Germany is not part of this approval.  

In this context, the Danish Energy Agency considers that the design of the project, with a focus on future-proofing, also addresses the need for integrating additional renewable energy and international connections. The layout of the station on Bornholm, which allows for expansion with more offshore wind and additional international connections, is therefore considered to fall within the scope of the network expansion requirements.  

Additionally, the Danish Energy Agency assesses that the project will contribute to creating well-functioning competitive markets by establishing a transmission network between Zealand and a presumed future price zone, Bornholm.  

Based on Energinet's application and business case, it has been concluded that the project is needed. The assessment has taken into account the socioeconomic consequences of the project.  

In light of this, the Minister for Climate, Energy, and Utilities has a favorable view of the project's necessity and will finalize the application once the project has been presented to the Climate, Energy, and Utilities Committee.

In 2020, a potential expansion to 3 GW was decided, and by the summer of 2022, the expansion of the wind farms to a capacity of 3 GW was officially approved. The two wind farms are located southwest of Bornholm.

840. ID: 1563
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Private person
   Statement: Energy islands are essentially expensive offshore transformers that collect and condition electricity from offshore wind turbines. These islands do not produce energy but instead consume energy in the process. Electricity from wind turbines, which convert only 10% to 30% of raw wind power into electricity, is sent to the energy island and converted from alternating current to direct current, resulting in about a 15% energy loss. This electricity is then transmitted via undersea cables to land, where it is converted back to alternating current, causing another 15% loss, before being sent to customers. Denmark, for example, generates more electricity by burning American wood chips as biomass than from all its wind turbines and solar panels combined. Globally, over the past decade, more than $5 trillion has been spent on the energy transition, yet wind and solar power contribute less than 5% of total energy consumption—a small achievement while economies face financial strain.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

863. ID: 4353
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)

   Statement: Denmark, together with the other Baltic Sea countries, has committed to increasing electricity generation from offshore wind in the Baltic Sea sevenfold by 2030. This agreement, outlined in the Marienborg Declaration, represents a significant step toward strengthening energy collaboration across the region.  

The decision is driven by the urgent need to free Europe from dependence on Russian gas, especially following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Energy has been weaponized, leading to an energy crisis, high prices, and inflation across Europe. It is essential to take all necessary steps to end this reliance and secure a sustainable energy future.  

The agreement includes increasing offshore wind capacity in the Baltic Sea from nearly 3 gigawatts to almost 20 gigawatts by 2030. This will involve installing between 1,100 and 1,700 wind turbines, providing enough electricity for up to 20 million European households. The potential for offshore wind in the Baltic Sea is enormous—up to 93 gigawatts by 2050, as estimated by the European Commission.  

Ending reliance on Russian gas is critical, as continued use of energy resources from an aggressor not only endangers security but also finances war. The Marienborg Declaration is a decisive step in ensuring Europe’s energy independence and addressing the climate crisis. By prioritizing green energy solutions, including hybrid projects connecting offshore wind farms across borders, it will be possible to cut CO₂ emissions and stabilize electricity prices, which are heavily affected by gas.  

This commitment builds on previous agreements, such as the Esbjerg Declaration, where North Sea countries agreed to expand offshore wind capacity tenfold. Together, these initiatives demonstrate that the Baltic Sea countries are determined to lead the way in renewable energy and energy security for Europe.

872. ID: 956
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Tenergy engineer
   Statement: I believe the chemical and steel industries in southern Sweden, along with the extensive Belgian and German industries, are key hubs for hydrogen consumption. In my view, Germany can produce about two-thirds of its own hydrogen needs but still depends on imports from Denmark to meet its total demand. Similarly, I see Sweden and Belgium as net importers of hydrogen, primarily relying on Denmark, while Sweden also sources some hydrogen from Poland.

I think hydrogen demand projections are often overly optimistic in the short and medium term. In my opinion, the buildout of hydrogen capacity is driven more by strategic decisions than by actual feasibility. I also believe models that rely on exogenous demand fail to account for this behavior. We need to be cautious when incorporating national strategies into multinational models, as these strategies can conflict and influence the model's outcomes. From my perspective, the North Sea is the most cost-effective place to produce hydrogen within the model. However, I recognize that the complexity of fuel trade is not fully captured in our model.

878. ID: 5112
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Private person
   Statement: The Danish plans to construct 10,000 wind turbines in the North Sea raise serious concerns about their impact on fishing grounds and the livelihoods of those in the fishing industry. These massive offshore wind farms could have significant consequences for Danish fisheries if not carefully managed.  

The proposed turbines must be situated outside the 30% of Danish fishing zones where fishing is permitted. Additionally, legislation should allow fishing near the turbines, as fish stocks tend to migrate. Furthermore, all cables from the turbines must be buried at least half a meter below the seabed to prevent damage from fishing equipment like trawls.  

If these measures are not implemented, there is a risk of increased unemployment among fishermen and fish processing workers, along with higher fish prices for the public. Addressing these concerns is crucial to balance renewable energy goals with the sustainability of Denmark's fishing industry.

Beyond Denmark, Ørsted is collaborating on major wind energy projects across Europe. 896. ID: 1710
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Rasmus Errboe
   Statement: Together with ATP,  we have developed a proposal for the energy island that a political majority wants to establish in the North Sea. 

The proposal can be described as a model that can be built upon as needs or technology change. 

Specifically, ATP and Ørsted propose building a smaller version of an artificial island. It can then gradually be expanded with new modules, such as those that make it possible to send offshore wind energy to land. 

According to us, it can be compared to building with LEGO bricks, where one can build and build on top of a foundation. 

The fundamental idea of our proposal is that it should be modular 

You build a relatively small enclosed island, where you then work with modules around the island that can be installed in connection with the island over time, as technological development changes.

925. ID: 2835
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Jakob Nørmark
   Statement: The introduction of a separate electricity price zone for Bornholm tied to the Energy Island will likely result in slightly cheaper electricity for Bornholm residents. However, this price difference is expected to be minimal. The new zone will only take effect if Bornholm’s grid is connected directly to the Energy Island's high-voltage infrastructure, enabling local access to offshore wind energy.  

If no such connection is established due to complexity or cost, Bornholm will remain part of the existing eastern Denmark (DK2) price zone, and an offshore price zone will instead cover only the wind farms and island infrastructure. In this scenario, Bornholm would continue to rely solely on its cable connection to Sweden.  

The purpose of the new price zone is to make the limitations of the transmission capacity between Bornholm, Zealand, and Germany visible to the market. Without this, the market could mistakenly assume that unlimited energy transfers are possible, leading to imbalances and costly corrective measures for Energinet, and by extension, the Danish public.  

The expected price benefit arises from market mechanisms where Bornholm’s spot price will align with the lowest neighboring price—either Zealand’s or Germany’s—depending on capacity availability. However, the price differences between these regions are usually minor. Under normal circumstances, the spot price only constitutes about 23% of the total consumer electricity bill, with taxes and tariffs making up the majority. Therefore, a lower wholesale price will only marginally impact overall consumer costs.  

Certain conditions, such as maintenance or cable damage, could cause energy production to exceed cable capacity, leading to temporarily lower prices on Bornholm. Conversely, if offshore wind production is low and cables are fully utilized, Bornholm’s price could match the higher German rates.  

Ultimately, the effect of a new price zone will depend on the evolving structure of the Energy Island project, such as additional wind capacity or the construction of large electricity-consuming facilities like power-to-X plants, which could either decrease or increase local electricity prices accordingly.

976. ID: 5275

   Statement: Denmark and Germany have signed a milestone agreement for Energy Island Bornholm, with Germany now investing in the infrastructure to transport electricity from Energy Island Bornholm to the German market via an undersea power cable running from Bornholm's high-voltage facility to Germany.

Energy islands, which will be located in the Baltic Sea at Bornholm and in the North Sea with an artificial island, are designed to significantly increase the production of renewable energy. The concept of energy islands involves setting up an infrastructure capable of producing renewable energy at a much larger scale. 984. ID: 5330

   Statement: The new geopolitical and energy market landscape has accelerated the green transition. The European Commission's RePowerEU plan aims to make Europe independent from Russian fossil fuels by 2030, prioritizing renewable energy, energy efficiency, and diversification. Combined with the European Green Deal and NextGenerationEU (NGEU) funding, these initiatives form a powerful foundation for sustainable energy development. However, islands face a unique energy challenge.

Islands struggle with higher electricity generation costs, often ten times greater than on the mainland, due to their size, isolation, and reliance on fossil fuel imports. They are also more prone to power outages. Despite these challenges, islands have long pursued sustainable solutions, driven by innovation, collaboration, and community effort, frequently utilizing cutting-edge technology. In many ways, islands serve as testing grounds for sustainable practices that could be scaled to larger, mainland communities. As the world grapples with the energy crisis, islands offer a potential blueprint for overcoming energy challenges.

They propose that Denmark could instead rely on green technologies, such as wind and solar energy, to ensure energy security without continuing fossil fuel production.

Despite this, Minister Dan Jørgensen maintains that Denmark has already set ambitious goals and is pushing for other countries to follow suit in establishing clear targets for phasing out fossil fuels. He emphasizes that Denmark's current stance and action plan are consistent with the global need for climate action, while calling for others to adopt similar measures in order to meet global climate targets.

On Zealand, the infrastructure will involve underground cables, potential reinforcements to the existing high-voltage grid, and a new high-voltage station that links the electricity from Energy Island Bornholm to the 400 kV transmission grid. 1035. ID: 5577
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Council on Climate Change
   Statement: Denmark can maintain high electricity supply security even under extreme weather conditions, despite the European electricity system increasingly relying on solar and wind energy. This security can be ensured through straightforward measures without significantly raising overall electricity supply costs. These measures include making electricity consumption more flexible, storing energy, and investing in reserve capacity for critical situations. 

However, the transformation of the energy system will place greater pressure on electricity supply security due to a significant increase in electricity consumption and the growing reliance on solar and wind energy, which cannot be regulated as easily as traditional power plants. By 2040, nearly all Danish electricity production will come from renewable sources, and electricity consumption will rise substantially, driven by national and EU policies to expand offshore wind and solar power while electrifying a significant portion of energy use. 

The challenges to electricity supply security are manageable, but implementing the necessary solutions—such as flexible consumption, energy storage, and reserve capacity—will take many years. Authorities must act promptly to address these challenges to avoid potential electricity shortages during peak demand periods when renewable sources cannot meet inflexible consumption. Ensuring supply security requires robust planning, including addressing reliance on varying energy sources, diminished dispatchable power plant capacity, and uncertain availability of electricity imports during stressed conditions.

1049. ID: 5694
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Andreas Wenzel
   Statement: The agreement encompasses a total of 9 gigawatts (GW) of offshore wind capacity, with the potential to expand to 14 GW or more. Currently, Denmark has 2.3 GW of offshore wind capacity in its waters. The agreement includes 6 GW of regular offshore wind farms and an additional 3 GW linked to the "Energy Island Bornholm Project." 

For the first time, the agreement establishes state co-ownership of offshore wind farms, with the Danish state and citizens holding a 20% stake. While this milestone is significant, it has sparked debates over the potential complexity and delays in the bidding process. The agreement sets a strict timeline for constructing the wind turbines by 2030.

The "Energy Island Bornholm Project" requires state support to be realized. Politicians have allocated up to 17.6 billion DKK in subsidies to cover the costs of an onshore facility on Bornholm and a high-capacity transmission cable connecting Bornholm, Zealand, and Germany. Germany will contribute its share and partially fund the onshore facility. However, the wind turbines themselves will be constructed without financial support.

This agreement represents a major step in the energy transition, ensuring the generation of significant amounts of green electricity for Denmark, Germany, and the rest of Europe.

1056. ID: 4318
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Miljøstyrelsen
   Statement: We at the Danish Environmental Protection Agency explain that, following this supplementary consultation, the landfall point at Vallø Strand has been excluded, and the cable route from Snoldelev-Hastrup to Vallø Strand has been removed. These changes reduce the cable system's length from approximately 30 km to around 8 km. The project now includes five specific landfall points on Bornholm with corresponding cable corridors leading to the station area, amounting to approximately 11 km of cable.

The cables will be installed as underground cables leading to the new high-voltage stations. For most sections, the cables will be buried, but in particularly sensitive areas, such as at watercourse crossings or vulnerable natural sites, the cables will be laid using directional drilling to avoid excavation and minimize environmental impact.

The environmental impacts of the cable-laying on land will primarily occur during the construction phase. These impacts are being studied, described, and assessed in the project's environmental impact report. This includes detailed studies and descriptions of specific areas along the route where construction must take special precautions due to terrain, nature, archaeological sites, soil conditions, landowner requirements, technical installations, or other spatial restrictions.

The impacts related to the establishment of land-based facilities will mainly occur within the project area. However, there may be effects beyond the project area, such as visual and noise-related impacts in nearby surroundings.

1058. ID: 5598
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: Yes, it is true that both Energinet and the agreement group have approved the possibility of Chinese cables being used in Denmark, but this is contingent on the fulfillment of specific requirements. The upcoming offshore wind auctions will allow both European and non-European companies, including Chinese companies, to participate, provided they meet the tender conditions. However, the actual suppliers of components, such as cables, are not part of the auction process. The winner of the auction (the concessionaire) can select their own suppliers, including those of cables, for the wind farm construction.

For the future wind auctions, there will be conditions that must be met, including new access requirements. These will include compliance with social clauses, such as the obligation to provide apprenticeship opportunities and prevent social dumping. Furthermore, there will be requirements to adhere to human rights and international conventions. The principle of chain responsibility will also be introduced, meaning that the concessionaire will be accountable for ensuring both their own compliance and that of their suppliers when working in Denmark. Additionally, sustainability requirements will be enforced, such as ensuring that concessionaires obtain third-party verified environmental product declarations for key components, including cables, from their suppliers.

I see tremendous development potential for Bornholm, particularly in creating an industrial park focused on green businesses connected to the energy island. This would enable the development, testing, demonstration, and export of new energy solutions.

To achieve this, we must ensure an attractive environment for investors—a thriving development ecosystem.

Today’s discussion must focus concretely on how we can establish initiatives such as a green industrial park and how we can further develop Rønne Harbour to support this vision.

1108. ID: 4576
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The realization of the Energy Island Bornholm plan may impact material assets, as the plan allows for the establishment of onshore facilities in areas previously used for other purposes. This could affect the use of existing areas for activities such as resource extraction, agriculture, infrastructure, or residential properties. Any impact will be closely tied to future land-use restrictions. It is expected that regular agricultural activities can continue under certain conditions related to the operation of future cable installations.

The plan is assessed to have no significant impact on commercial and residential areas, as the designated zones for land cables and high-voltage facilities largely avoid these areas. However, isolated properties may be affected in connection with future specific projects.

On Zealand, the land cable corridors align mostly with the existing 400 kV high-voltage line corridor and are therefore not expected to impose additional significant restrictions on buildings or other infrastructure. On Bornholm, there are no conflicts with existing infrastructure.

The designated areas on Bornholm and Zealand overlap with agricultural zones and a few small resource extraction areas, which can be avoided during the planning of specific projects.

Overall, it is considered feasible to locate the high-voltage facilities and cables on Bornholm and Zealand in a way that avoids significant impacts on material assets.

1109. ID: 4574
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The realization of the Energy Island Bornholm plan has the potential to affect soil conditions due to the possibility of municipalities altering land use within the planned areas. These potential effects on soil include land appropriation, soil compaction, contamination, and changes to groundwater levels. Experience from similar projects shows that soil impact is most significant during the establishment of high-voltage installations, while the impacts of laying land cables are temporary and less severe.

On both Bornholm and Zealand, there are significant areas with freshwater formations within the planning zones for high-voltage installations. These areas will be further investigated to identify potential deep peat and organic soil zones as part of specific construction considerations. It is assessed that the construction enabled by the plan can proceed without significant impacts.

There are no extensive areas with identified soil contamination within the planned zones for land cables and high-voltage installations. The construction enabled by the plan is considered feasible without a risk of increased contamination spread, including to groundwater, provided any contaminated soil is managed according to current legislation. The risk of increased soil contamination is deemed low, as contaminated sites can be avoided, and any affected soil will be handled according to established guidelines. Overall, it is assessed that there will be no significant impact on soil from the realization of the plan.

On Zealand, several parts of the planned zones for land cables and the landing of submarine cables overlap with lowland areas identified in municipal plans. Guided drilling is used to install cables under lowland areas, which minimizes significant impacts. However, establishing high-voltage installations and other fixed facilities, such as joint bays, on lowland areas may require additional drainage, potentially leading to ochre leakage. Despite this, it is possible to place joint bays outside designated lowland areas to avoid such impacts. High-voltage installations can also be established outside lowland areas on both Zealand and Bornholm. Consequently, the impact on lowland areas is assessed as negligible, and the overall effect is not considered significant.

1110. ID: 4573
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: We acknowledges that the implementation of the Energy Island Bornholm program may impact recreational interests, including tourism. Such impacts could arise if the allocation of areas under the plan limits public access to recreational zones or directly or indirectly diminishes the recreational value of these areas. High-voltage installations may cause permanent impacts, while impacts from land cables and shoreline cable landings are considered temporary.

Specific recreational interests have been identified in areas designated for high-voltage installations and land cables on both Bornholm and Zealand. On Bornholm, the placement of high-voltage installations near the Læså area could conflict with its recreational value, causing visual and noise disturbances, which render the area highly sensitive. Similarly, on Zealand, high-voltage installations primarily affect agricultural land and the recreational area of Solhøj Fælled, but suitable placements that avoid these impacts are also considered feasible.

In areas designated for land cables and shoreline cable landings on both Bornholm and Zealand, several recreational interests exist. Controlled horizontal drilling techniques will be used to route cables beneath sensitive areas, such as coastlines and forests, which are expected to result in negligible impacts on recreational interests. Consequently, the implementation of these components is not anticipated to have a significant effect. However, cumulative effects from the realization of the Ring 5 in the Finger Plan combined with the Energy Island Bornholm program are expected to significantly and negatively affect recreational interests on Zealand.

1112. ID: 4571
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The plan for the Energy Island Bornholm project enables the establishment of high-voltage facilities for the distribution and transformation of electricity from offshore wind farms connected to Energy Island Bornholm on both Bornholm and Zealand. These high-voltage facilities are significant technical installations that will visually impact the landscapes in which they are placed. Depending on their location and design, the facilities will vary in visibility.

The landscapes within the planned areas for high-voltage facilities and land cables on Bornholm and Zealand are assessed as having high and medium vulnerability, respectively. These areas contain landscape qualities and conservation values but are already influenced by other large technical installations, such as high-voltage masts on Zealand and existing onshore wind turbines on Bornholm.

The potential visual impact of the high-voltage facilities on the landscapes of Bornholm and Zealand is assessed as high. The facilities will be dominant elements in landscapes currently characterized primarily by agricultural activities. Whether established as AIS or GIS facilities, their size and scale will make them very prominent. The visual impact on Zealand is assessed as significant overall.

The potential impact on the landscape and visual conditions will be limited to the immediate vicinity, as the facilities will not be visible over long distances due to terrain slopes, existing buildings, and vegetation. The visual impact can be mitigated through screening vegetation, terrain modeling, or the establishment of earthen embankments with a shielding effect.

On Bornholm, it is considered feasible to locate high-voltage facilities within the planned area without significantly affecting key landscape elements, making the visual impact from the project insignificant. 

The project will involve the placement of cables and jointing pits between submarine and land cables on Bornholm and Zealand. This will require clearing areas around the cables to remove plants, trees with deep roots, and buildings. The jointing pits will consist of wells with a maximum height of 0.5 meters above ground level. The visual and landscape impact of these land and submarine cables will be limited. Directional drilling will be used for cable installations crossing forests and valuable hedgerows. No jointing pits will be constructed above ground in areas where this would conflict with landscape protection, such as within shoreline protection zones or protected areas. In these locations, the visual impact will be negligible, and the establishment of cables and landings will not significantly affect visual conditions.

However, the realization of the Ring 5 in the Finger Plan, in combination with the Energy Island Bornholm project, is expected to have a substantial negative impact on the landscape interests and visual character of Zealand.

1113. ID: 4570
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The water quality in Køge Bugt and the Baltic Sea near Bornholm is currently in poor ecological condition due to nutrient overload originating from surrounding land areas. Additionally, these marine areas are not in good chemical condition due to elevated levels of pollutants in the seabed sediments.

The Water Framework Directive sets targets for achieving good ecological and chemical status by 2027, while Denmark’s Marine Strategy establishes objectives for reducing eutrophication and limiting pollutant concentrations in the sea, as well as in seafood used for consumption.

The implementation of the Energy Island Bornholm Program Plan will not lead to additional nutrient or pollutant inputs into the marine areas. The construction of offshore wind farms and buried cables may cause temporary, short-term seabed disturbances, but these are not expected to degrade water quality to the extent that the overall ecological status would be compromised. Additionally, the planned offshore wind development will not hinder the Marine Strategy's goals of reduced eutrophication and pollutant levels.

In terms of the Water Framework Directive's requirements for ensuring good ecological and chemical status, it is assessed that the realization of the Energy Island Bornholm Program Plan will not have a significant impact on water quality and will not prevent the achievement of these objectives.

Regarding the potential impacts on the overarching objectives of the Marine Strategy Directive, it is concluded that achieving or maintaining good environmental status in Danish marine areas will not be significantly affected by the implementation of the Energy Island Bornholm Program Plan. Consequently, the degree of impact is assessed to be negligible, and the influence on water quality is therefore not significant.

1127. ID: 4566

   Statement: The realization of the Energy Island Bornholm Plan may lead to potential impacts on fish and fish populations due to habitat changes and displacement from living areas caused by increased sediment in the water column. The construction of foundations on the seabed and the laying of submarine cables could result in permanent and temporary alterations to the seabed, potentially affecting feeding grounds, spawning areas, and nursery habitats for fish. During construction activities such as foundation excavation and cable laying, increased concentrations of suspended sediment in the water column may occur, which could displace fish that rely on vision for hunting and feeding. Overall, the impact level is assessed as insignificant, and the effect on fish populations is not considered significant.

The impact on fish due to habitat changes from the installation of turbines and cables is assessed as negligible and not significant, as the structures represent a limited area of the overall soft-bottom substrate. Excluding commercial fishing in the planned areas and along the cables is expected to have a small positive impact on local fish populations in the area. Consequently, the overall impact on fish is assessed as negligible and not significant. Fish potentially affected by EMF from buried submarine cables are only expected to experience minimal impacts, as the cables will be buried 1 meter below the seabed, and the EMF exposure at the surface is very low. This potential impact is assessed as being very localized, within a few meters of the cables, and of low intensity and permanent duration. Overall, the impact is considered negligible and not significant for fish populations.

1132. ID: 4578
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: We acknowledges that some components in high-voltage systems may contain potent greenhouse gases, such as SF6 (sulfur hexafluoride), commonly used in high-voltage components over 100 kV and as an insulating medium in Gas Insulated Switchgear (GIS). SF6 is a powerful greenhouse gas, 25,200 times more potent than CO₂ and with an atmospheric lifespan of 3,200 years. Emissions occur during filling, leaks, and similar processes.

The implementation of the Energy Island Bornholm program will enable the construction of high-voltage systems on Bornholm and Zealand, which may lead to unintended emissions of SF6 during operation. However, the anticipated emissions are assessed as having no significant climate impact due to their limited contribution relative to municipal and national carbon inventories. Over time, SF6 will be gradually replaced with alternatives that have a lower climate footprint. If future high-voltage systems are built using SF6 and the estimated emissions occur, the negative effects can be mitigated by utilizing agricultural land. Overall, the impact on the climate is expected to be minimal, and the plan's realization may result in a small net positive effect.

1133. ID: 6566
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Halonen et al.
   Statement: Norway's approach to energy transition presents a unique paradox. As a wealthy petro-state with strong social welfare systems, we've integrated sustainable development into our policies, but we haven't specifically tackled just transition in our energy policy discussions. Our welfare state heavily depends on petroleum revenues, and many assume our Oil Fund will simply carry us through the energy transition smoothly.

This assumption is problematic. We need to recognize that even wealthy Norway requires careful attention to justice in energy and climate policies. Currently, our just transition discussions are fragmented - they either focus solely on the oil and gas industry's needs or on specific communities' renewable energy projects. Instead, we need comprehensive national policies that address multiple aspects of justice: distributive, procedural, recognitive, and restorative.

Just as we've made sustainable development and SDGs fundamental to energy system planning, just transition principles need to be embedded at every policy level. This means expanding our focus on social aspects through community engagement in formal project development processes. The Storheia case demonstrates why we need participatory political processes that truly value local perspectives. However, we haven't yet realized the potential to address just transition at higher policymaking levels across multiple domains. Studying controversies can help us identify both the commonly addressed and neglected aspects of just transition, which should inform future policy development.

1147. ID: 962

   Statement: We acknowledge the critical importance of energy security and combating climate change for the future of the European Union. We recognize that recent geopolitical events have highlighted the urgent need to replace fossil fuels, especially Russian oil, coal, and gas, with European renewable energy from the North Sea, including offshore wind electricity and green hydrogen, to support both EU climate neutrality and energy security. 

We further acknowledge the cooperation established between Denmark, Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands in the “Esbjerg Declaration” of May 18th, 2022, which envisions the North Sea as a Green Power Plant of Europe. In our view, offshore renewable energy hubs and a meshed offshore grid are essential for generating, connecting, converting, and transporting offshore wind energy in the North Sea. 

We note Germany’s plans to establish offshore renewable energy clusters with a 10 GW capacity in the North Sea by the mid-2030s and Denmark’s plans to create a Danish Energy Island with up to 10 GW capacity by 2040. Additionally, we recall the EU Marine Strategy Directive and our joint commitment to achieving good environmental status for all European seas, including the North Sea.

We have agreed on the necessity of this Joint Declaration of Intent (JDoI) to focus on cooperation for connecting Germany’s planned offshore renewable energy hubs with Denmark’s Energy Island. Our primary objective is to facilitate mutual benefits by improving energy security, increasing socio-economic welfare, diversifying energy sources, meeting EU and national renewable energy targets, and integrating wind power with hydrogen and Power-to-X technologies.

To achieve this, we propose the establishment of a Joint Working Group led by energy ministries, supported by energy authorities and Transmission System Operators (TSOs). This group will develop a pre-feasibility study analyzing technical, environmental, and economic aspects and deliver a joint recommendation by the first half of 2024. This recommendation will guide the next steps toward realizing the project, aiming for implementation by the mid-2030s.

We emphasize that this JDoI creates no binding obligations under international law and imposes no financial commitments unless mutually agreed. Cooperation costs are borne by the respective Participant. Any amendments to this JDoI require joint written consent, and any misunderstandings will be resolved collaboratively in good faith and mutual trust. 

This JDoI takes effect upon signature and may be terminated with three months' written notice. Termination does not affect ongoing activities unless otherwise decided.

Signed on April 24th, 2023, in Ostende.

1157. ID: 4579

   Cluster: (None)

   Statement: To implement the Plan for Program Energiø Bornholm, cables may need to be installed through three Natura 2000 areas on land: N148 Køge Å, N149 Tryggevælde Å, and N187 Kystskrænter ved Arnager Bugt. A significance assessment has been conducted to evaluate potential impacts on these areas.

All cable installations within Natura 2000 areas will use guided horizontal drilling. The only potential impact identified is the risk of unintended drilling mud leaks. The significance assessment concludes that a significant impact on the designation basis of Natura 2000 area N187 can be ruled out because the habitat types within the area are not vulnerable to such leaks. Similarly, most habitat types and species in areas N148 and N149 are not vulnerable, but potential impacts on nutrient-rich lake habitats in N148 and lagoon habitats in N149 cannot be ruled out. Consequently, an impact assessment was conducted for these two habitat types.

Since the identified vulnerable habitats are small and located on the edges of the plan area, potential damage can be avoided by conducting drilling outside these sensitive habitats. The conclusion of the impact assessment is that the realization of the Plan for Program Energiø Bornholm, either individually or in combination with other projects, will not risk harming the habitat types in the Natura 2000 designation basis. This is contingent on implementing all relevant mitigation measures in future projects. Based on this, the integrity of the Natura 2000 areas will not be compromised by the implementation of the Plan for Program Energiø Bornholm on land.

1167. ID: 1180
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Peter K. Kruse-Andersen
   Statement: I highlight a coordination problem between the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and the EU's offshore renewable energy strategy. I exemplify this coordination failure by analyzing carbon leakage effects associated with Denmark's planned North Sea energy island. The Danish energy island project will not start production before 2033, implying a long interval between project announcement and production. Using a dynamic model of the EU ETS, I show that the large time gap between announcement and production likely results in a ‘Green Paradox’, where the energy island increases aggregate EU ETS emissions. The mechanism leading to the emission increase is complicated and works through the Market Stability Reserve (MSR). The estimated 2050 leakage rate is 145 percent in our main scenario and not below 100 percent in any alternative scenario. We discuss how to improve the climate benefits of the energy island or similar large-scale renewable energy projects. This includes possible revisions to the EU ETS and the role of Power-to-X technologies.

There is a coordination failure between the EU ETS and the EU's offshore renewable energy strategy, as projects intended to fulfil the offshore strategy are likely to result in substantial carbon leakage due to the EU ETS.
In ETS-covered sectors, there are averse leakage effects associated with emission abatement projects with significant time lags between project announcements and emission abatement like the Danish North Sea energy island.
For the North Sea energy island and similar projects, leakage effects can be diminished through policies that mitigate the impact on EU ETS allowance demand.
The coordination failure can be eliminated by removing MSR cancellations or the entire MSR mechanism while adjusting the emission cap to hold expected emissions constant.
However, removing MSR cancellations amplifies leakage effects for abatement projects with short time lags between announcements and emission abatement, which currently have weak leakage effects due to MSR cancellations.

1170. ID: 4550
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: Radar and radio communication are critical for civil and military purposes at sea and in the airspace. Offshore wind farms and other marine structures may potentially affect radar coverage and radio communication, including radio link systems, if positioned within their coverage areas. Radar and radio waves can be reflected or weakened, degrading the signals.

The weather radar on Bornholm is the only civilian radar system that could be impacted by offshore wind farms planned in the area. The impact could result in a radar shadow zone behind the wind turbines, where radar signals are disrupted, appearing as 'clutter' on the screen. This will moderately affect the radar system, but the overall impact is assessed as not significant.

Potential disruptions from offshore wind farms are expected to have minimal impact on the quality of coastal radio systems, as these systems do not rely on a single line-of-sight connection. Therefore, the impact on radio systems is considered insignificant.

The implementation of the plan may temporarily block the line of sight between two receivers in the Differential Global Positioning System (DGPS), leading to momentary signal degradation. This could delay the correction of a ship’s GPS position (which has an accuracy of ~10 meters, compared to ~0.1 meters for DGPS). However, this impact on telecommunication, VHF, and navigation systems is assessed as insignificant.

Military radar systems are not included in the environmental assessment. The Ministry of Defense is conducting a separate analysis regarding these systems.

The choice of production capacity configuration for offshore wind energy does not affect these conclusions.

1190. ID: 4560
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The Natura 2000 areas are designated based on European nature protection directives and are part of the EU's international network of habitat and bird protection areas. Each Natura 2000 area has a specific designation basis, listing habitat types and species meant for protection. 

The realization of the "Energy Island Bornholm Program Plan" may affect certain habitat types and species in several Natura 2000 areas. A materiality assessment was conducted for all relevant Natura 2000 areas, including those with migratory birds as part of their designation basis. This assessment incorporated standard noise-reduction measures in modeling underwater noise from pile driving. 

The conclusion of the materiality assessment is that significant displacement effects on harbor porpoises due to underwater noise cannot be ruled out. However, no other habitat types or species designated for protection would be significantly affected. 

A subsequent impact assessment for harbor porpoises, where significant effects could not initially be ruled out, concluded that the species would not be harmed if pile driving occurs no closer than 5–7 kilometers from the affected Natura 2000 areas during winter (November through April). In the summer, pile driving must not involve more than one foundation at a time near the habitat areas, as simultaneous pile driving could increase the area and duration of porpoise displacement.

The final conclusion of the impact assessment is that the realization of the "Energy Island Bornholm Program Plan," whether on its own or in combination with other projects, poses no risk of harm to harbor porpoises or the integrity of the Natura 2000 areas. This conclusion assumes the implementation of all relevant mitigation measures in future projects. Therefore, the integrity of Natura 2000 areas will not be compromised by the realization of the program plan.

1204. ID: 4554

   Statement: We acknowledges that the realization of the Energy Island Bornholm Program Plan poses a risk of encountering and impacting chemical and/or conventional weapons on the seabed. The planned areas intersect a known minefield southwest of Bornholm that was mined by the British Air Force during World War II. Additionally, the western part of the planning area overlaps with a former British minefield, German convoy routes from December 1944, and a potential impact area near Stevns Fortet.

The Bornholm II offshore wind turbine area intersects historical transport routes from German ports to dumping zones and borders areas where chemical weapons have previously been recorded. The planning area for subsea cables is adjacent to an emergency dumping zone southwest of Bornholm.

The rate of findings cannot be precisely determined until a specific project design is available and a geophysical screening survey of identified magnetic anomalies is conducted. It is critical that all necessary safety precautions are implemented when carrying out activities that may disturb the seabed. This includes ensuring that first aid equipment for chemical weapons exposure is always readily available.
