1218. ID: 7081
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Beirut International
   Statement: Offshore wind energy generation is more efficient than on land, to harness it you’d have to follow the wind. Ocean water currents offer a much higher energy density, at a stable rate, the technology is progressing, to harness you’d have to follow the currents. 
To make Hydrogen Green, sea water reverse osmosis and electrolysis equipment have to be close to an energy source, from here the idea of Energy Islands begins. 

Energy Islands should be near the winds, waves and currents. The Baltic Sea average depth is 50 m, the North Sea 90 m, the Mediterranean Sea 1,500 m, the Atlantic Ocean 3,600 m.

Energy Islands should be accessible all year long. Offshore rigs personnel have to go through extensive safety training to be allowed to make the trip by Helicopter or by Offshore Support Vessels, both ways are expensive and at high risk.
Energy Islands should cater for additional space when an Wind Farm expands; and permit ergonomic maintenance and replacement of equipment without the use of heavy lift Floating Marine Cranes and Floating Docks.

Energy Islands service and operations teams may range from dozens to hundreds. This team require fresh water supply, food supply, cold service water, hot service water, wastewater disposal, solid waste disposal and regular rotation.  Offshore supply and retrieval trips made by Offshore Supply Vessels is dangerous and expensive in high seas.

Supposing a nation wishes to build an Energy Island by backfilling into the sea within its economic water zone; the currents within this sea would have to be studied not to alter direction and affect neighboring nations, the sediments from the backfilling process would be carried to undesirable locations within the nation shoreline, or to neighboring shoreline, affecting marine fauna and flora. A thorough Environmental Impact Assessment should be endorsed by all nation stakeholders.
Assuming an EIA is approved, lets look at the backfilling process on a sandy bed at 50 m seawater depth. If the surface footprint of the island is to be 500m x 500m, the scour protection measures, whatever the method used, would have a footprint of around 600m x 600m at sea bed level. The offshore contracting operations would have to be carried out within the yearly calm season, if the entire operation, or the milestone target construction is not achieved within the first season, the sea would destroy and remove most of it before the next season.
 After completion, if a structural failure occurs, under rough sea conditions, repairs would have to wait till the calm season, at the risk of further uncontrollable damage.
Once such Energy Island is completed, installing equipment on top would follow any port procedures; if certain components need to be replaced, they would have to be lifted and transported onto a vessel.
While this enormous offshore marine contracting job maybe concluded at 50m depth, will let the reader imagine the 90m or 1,500m sea depth scenario feasibility.

A Floating Island is fabricated in a shipyard, launched to sea, tugged to the desired location, and anchored. The process is carried in a controlled environment, irrespective of sea state and sea depth.
While many Floating Island solutions are marketed, and most developers submitted their design to the UN Habitat in 2018 in a New York meeting, none of their literature is conclusive, most of it is at conceptual level. 
The only solution that passed Two Marine Societies design approval by Bureau Veritas  in 2005 and International Naval Survey Bureau in 2009, and a thorough Marine Society design, engineering, procurement and fabrication survey by INSB from 2009 till 2015 is the one made by Dr. Abdullah Daou, the founder of Beirut International Marine Industry and Commerce. 
Beirut International’s Floating Island first prototype was made in 1997, at a scale of 1:10 measuring 4m x 4m, was extensively tested in a make shift water basin, with better than expected stability results under high simulated waves condition.

In 2009 the fabrication of the first Floating Island made by Beirut International started in Lebanon. The substructure base 48m wide, by 76m long, 9m deep and weighing around 4,000 tons was being assembled in Tripoli Shipyard, while structural components where being fabricated in three other workshops in Lebanon by a team of 431 local technicians and engineers. 
While the fate of this structure was unfortunate, Ninety-Eight Million US Dollars were invested in the research, development and fabrication; a 70% completion rate was achieved, almost all drawings approved and stamped by INSB meeting SOLAS and other marine regulations. 
The learning curve is priceless. The technology is ready, far ahead of any contender. True, a full-scale prototype is yet to be made again and tested.


There is seven pros for building the energy islands.
A Floating Energy Island is modular, making it scalable to meet any Offshore Wind Farm expansion. If maintenance is requires, a module can be detached, tugged to a shipyard then re-connected.
The substructure of a Floating Energy Island is transparent to the sea, making it an artificial coral reef for marine life, and simultaneously providing anchoring points to install Water Current Energy makers. 
The waves are absorbed and damped by the Floating Energy Island, creating a calm water area at the rear port for Vessel to approach and dock at ease, allowing for safe and friendly access. 
Being a generator of Hydrogen, and having a large underwater space, it is an ideal location to develop sustainable fisheries, creating an additional export income.
Solid waste composting and wastewater treatment available technologies can make some agriculture a sustainable alternative to waste disposal.
The Hydrogen process being noiseless, and clean; a Yacht Club can be safe haven for yachts sailing across seas and oceans.

However the cons of building the islands are yet to be tested by our firm.

The Hydrogen Environment is relatively new. 
Stakeholders include: Shipping Companies, Energy Companies, Ports Logistics, Telecommunication, Reverse Osmosis Water Makers, Electroliser Makers, Wind Turbine makers, Wave Energy Makers, Current Energy Makers, Shipyards, Marine Offshore Contractors, Hydrogen Storage Solution Makers, Inverters, Controls, Aquaponics, Wastewater Treatment, Solid Waste Treatment… 
While some stakeholders are more advanced then the other, some at prototyping stage, other at maturity; a Floating Energy Island success needs their close collaboration. A fresh firm in the Legal field is trying to advise stakeholders to join efforts and Joint Venture to make such infrastructure and energy concepts a needed reality to meet a Marine Decarbonization.

1295. ID: 617
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: We state that, as part of the Climate Agreement for energy and industry, Denmark has decided to develop two energy islands: one in the North Sea and one in the Baltic Sea near Bornholm. These energy islands are a key component of the expansion of offshore wind in both the North and Baltic Seas and are expected to play a significant role in Denmark's and Europe's green transition.

It has been politically decided that the Energy Island near Bornholm must be located at least 15 kilometers from the coast, with a minimum capacity of 3 GW of offshore wind power, with the potential for an additional 800 MW of overcapacity, bringing the total capacity to up to 3.8 GW.

The Energy Island near Bornholm will consist of offshore facilities in the Baltic Sea, including wind turbines with internal seabed cables, offshore transformer platforms, and seabed cables connecting the wind farms to Bornholm and from Bornholm to Zealand, as well as an international connection to Germany. On land, there will be land-based facilities on Bornholm (buried land cables and a high-voltage station) and in Solhøj, Zealand (buried land cables and a high-voltage station).

1308. ID: 869
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Journalist
   Statement: While researchers may calculate that it is theoretically possible to base energy supply on wind and solar power, I believe it is not desirable for several reasons.

First, there will inevitably be numerous challenges in translating theory into practice, leading to delays in the energy transition and prolonged dependence on fossil fuels.

Second, Power-to-X technology is not yet mature, and there are no facilities currently capable of delivering the scale of energy needed to power an entire country. Politicians are gambling on the rapid development of this technology, but there is no guarantee it will be ready when needed. Additionally, storing and transporting large quantities of energy for periods with no wind or solar power—such as calm, foggy weeks in January—presents significant logistical challenges.

The North Sea Energy Island is projected to cost 210 billion kroner, providing an installed capacity of 3 GW of wind turbines, with an actual average output of 1.5 GW due to a capacity factor of 50%. This must cover electricity consumption, Power-to-X needs, and electrified district heating. The Energy Island is not expected to be operational until 2033. By comparison, Poland has agreed to purchase six APR 1400 nuclear reactors from South Korea’s Kepco for 202 billion kroner, providing 8.4 GW installed capacity and 7.98 GW effective output due to a 95% capacity factor. The first reactor is expected to deliver electricity to the Polish grid by 2030. Nuclear power can also provide district heating, reducing the need for additional electricity. Given Denmark’s energy needs of 4–5 GW, the Polish model would offer surplus capacity for exports, synthetic fuels, or cost savings by building fewer reactors.

A wind- and solar-powered grid would require substantial technological solutions, such as using electric vehicle batteries to buffer fluctuations. A stable supply from nuclear power would eliminate the need for these costly and unnecessary innovations, reduce wear on expensive batteries, and avoid changing consumption habits—arguably one of the most challenging tasks.

It has been documented that wind power requires more than twice the resources (concrete, steel, copper, etc.) to deliver the same amount of energy as nuclear power.

Denmark currently imports hydropower from Norway during shortages, but Norway has faced decreasing rainfall in recent years, limiting its ability to export electricity. Norwegian energy officials have also stated that Norway neither can nor wishes to serve as a buffer for Northern Europe. Even Norway is debating nuclear power due to doubts about the long-term reliability of hydropower.

In summary, while it might be theoretically possible to rely on wind and solar power, I do not believe there is sufficient time to develop, build, and implement the necessary solutions or to change consumption habits. This approach risks prolonging our reliance on fossil fuels such as coal or deforestation-based biomass.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1309. ID: 361
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: WindEurope
   Statement: The North Sea has the potential to host more than 200 offshore wind farms, each with a capacity of 1 GW, due to its strong winds and shallow waters. However, achieving this requires building wind farms far from the coast, which significantly increases the cost of electrical infrastructure. Alternating current does not transmit efficiently over long distances, necessitating the use of more expensive direct current substations and cabling.

Building an energy island transforms this scenario. An energy island allows for the pooling of electrical infrastructure—such as transformers and cables—connecting the wind farms to the mainland, thereby reducing the required investment. Additionally, an energy island enables the delivery of electricity to multiple countries instead of a single national grid. This makes it easier to sell electricity at the best price when wind farms are operating at full capacity, without risking instability in any single grid.

This must happen in cooperation between the state and the business sector. And it will be very concrete: The agreement parties agree that the state should be a co-owner of the individual offshore wind farms. To ensure that the Danish society gets a fair share of future revenues when our shared maritime resource is used for offshore wind. Co-ownership is a stamp of confidence for developers that the government wants to invest in the green transition – together with them and for the benefit of society as a whole,” says Minister for Business Morten Bødskov.

1334. ID: 2296
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Financial viability and (un)profitability
   Actor: John Ammentorp
   Statement: Energy islands are strategically vital and economically sound investments for several key reasons. The Danish North Sea energy island project will make energy more affordable by creating near-shore environments for far-offshore wind farms. By placing wind farms closer to energy islands instead of the mainland, the Danish North Sea energy island will reduce complexity and costs by minimizing or eliminating long underwater cable runs to shore.

Energy islands provide crucial flexibility in Denmark's renewable energy system. The Danish North Sea energy island will serve as an accumulation point for surplus energy during high-production periods and enable strategic distribution during peak demand times. This capability directly addresses the challenge of balancing renewable energy production with consumption.

The costs for the Danish North Sea energy island fall into three main categories:
1. Capital expenditures for physical infrastructure construction, including the artificial island itself and electrical infrastructure
2. Operational costs that vary based on design choices, technology selection, geographic location, and project scale
3. Technology development costs, particularly for high-voltage direct current equipment and Power-to-X systems

1335. ID: 5984

   Statement: In collaboration with a range of other nations,
Denmark has committed to a massive increase in
renewable energy production. For the North Seas
alone, a 300 GW (Giga Watt) wind power capacity
has been agreed for 2050. In comparison, the total
Danish offshore wind power capacity today is 2.3 GW.
Meeting these commitments through near-shore
wind power parks alone will just not be possible.
Even if existing local planning and protests from
citizens were disregarded, the available space
would fall short by a large margin. Thus, the
build-out needs to be based on the use of the
open sea wind resource.
Fortunately, the potential for open sea wind power
production is huge. However, the technical setup
around near-shore wind power parks cannot be
transferred to the open sea. At today’s near-shore
parks, power is produced as an alternating current
(AC) and transmitted directly to shore. This would
not work for an open sea park. Due to the longer
distance, the power must be converted into a
direct current (DC). The space requirements for the
converters and related equipment demand housing
at a physical structure close to the production site.
In other words, a build-out of the scale in question
would be impossible without energy islands.

Our calculations show that the impact will be minimal if Bornholm only serves as a service port for the energy island and maximal if a Power-to-X (PtX) facility is also established. Approximately half of the new jobs and population increase associated with Energy Island Bornholm will only materialize if a PtX facility, based on a 3GW hydrogen production plant, is constructed. 
A PtX facility would also create localized by-products, such as surplus heat, which could attract new businesses that utilize this surplus heat in their operations. These additional socioeconomic effects have not been included in our current calculations and should be added to the presented figures. The dimensions of the calculated PtX facility are based on the original plans associated with two open-door projects already underway on Bornholm. Other effects of these open-door projects were not included in this analysis. 
Based on experience from Energy Island calculations, we estimate that fully realizing the open-door projects would lead to an additional 590 new residents, resulting in a total migration increase of over 1,600 individuals if both the energy island and open-door projects are implemented. If the electricity from the energy island is used for PtX production, the total migration is expected to be approximately 1,060 individuals. However, this estimate does not include potential employment and migration resulting from the greening of Bornholm’s economy or the emergence of new green industries. These effects are addressed in a separate report focusing on the further development of Bornholm as a testing hub for energy technology.

1354. ID: 2143
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Center for Regional and Tourism Research
   Statement: The construction of Energy Island Bornholm will require significant construction work, necessitating the temporary accommodation of a large workforce. It is not yet clear how the various contractors will address this need. We estimate approximately 5,300 annual work units of temporary labor will be involved in the construction phase of Energy Island Bornholm. This employment is not permanent but is noteworthy because it generates consumption linked to these work units, creating additional turnover on Bornholm and fostering local employment.
The temporary workforce will exhibit a consumption level and pattern different from that of the permanent residents and the typical Bornholm tourist. This workforce is expected to spend on daily goods, retail products, entertainment, dining, transportation, and similar services. However, it remains difficult to determine the exact local spending levels. 
Based on SKAT’s tax deduction guidelines for dual household maintenance during work assignments, we have assumed an average daily expenditure of 555 DKK per person as a baseline consumption estimate. Over the construction period, this workforce is projected to spend a total of 662 million DKK. The impact of this spending is referred to as temporary, derived employment in our tables and graphs, resulting in an additional 135 annual work units of local employment.

1355. ID: 2148
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Center for Regional and Tourism Research
   Statement: Experience from other large construction projects, such as the Fehmarn Belt project, suggests that a significant portion of the temporary workforce may be housed in temporary barrack towns. It is also possible that accommodation will partly rely on the existing hospitality sector, including summer houses, holiday centers, campsites, hotels, hotel ships, or standard apartments across Bornholm. If some of the workforce is housed within the existing tourism sector, it will likely put pressure on Bornholm's tourism revenue. 
Due to the high productivity and income-generating capacity of the wind energy industry, demand for accommodations could displace current tourists. While this would improve profitability for accommodation providers, the lower daily spending patterns of construction workers compared to tourists would likely lead to reduced revenue, profits, and tax contributions from sectors that serve tourists. 
To avoid directly impacting Bornholm's tourism sector, we assume that the temporary workforce will primarily be housed in barrack towns. However, this assumption also means that accommodation and rental income will not contribute to Bornholm's economy.

1378. ID: 2593
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Peter K. Kruse-Andersena
   Statement: I highlight a coordination problem between the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and the EU's offshore renewable energy strategy, using Denmark's planned North Sea energy island as an example. The long gap between the project's announcement and its start in 2033 could lead to a 'Green Paradox,' where emissions actually increase in the EU ETS due to the way the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) functions. My study shows that the leakage rate in 2050 could be as high as 145%, and I suggest potential solutions to improve the climate benefits of large-scale projects like this. These include revising the EU ETS or utilizing Power-to-X technologies, though these won't fully resolve the coordination failure. One option is removing the MSR or adjusting the emission cap to give politicians more control over long-term emissions, but this could increase leakage effects and price volatility. In conclusion, there is no easy solution to this problem.

1385. ID: 4348
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Financial viability and (un)profitability
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: The North Sea energy island project has encountered significant financial challenges. The project, which was supposed to serve as a hub for collecting and distributing electricity from offshore wind turbines located 80–100 kilometers off the west coast of Jutland, is currently estimated to cost the state over 50 billion kroner. This far exceeds the acceptable level of financial viability required by the political agreements that underpin the project.

Given these economic obstacles, the Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities will spend the next six months exploring alternative designs to make the project less complex and more affordable. The current model, developed since 2020, has proven to be too costly and risky. To address these issues, I, Lars Aagaard, Minister for Climate, Energy, and Utilities, am considering lessons from other North Sea countries. These countries have opted for simpler steel structure platforms to reduce costs. Another potential cost-saving measure involves accelerating the construction of some offshore wind turbines, which would generate power for the energy island sooner.

Despite the delays, the government remains committed to the ambition of realizing the North Sea energy island. However, adjustments must be made to ensure the project is economically viable. It is essential to move quickly, as the energy island needs to be operational shortly after 2030 to meet energy goals. We will engage in discussions with businesses, investors, and the Danish Parliament to find viable solutions and proceed responsibly without unnecessary haste.

The challenges are significant, but they reflect the scale and innovation required for a project of this nature, which has never been attempted before.

1387. ID: 2691
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: The Climate, Energy, and Utilities Committee has asked me, in a letter dated June 1, 2023, to answer the following question, which was requested by Steffen W. Frølund (LA). The question concerns the consequences of applying the same tariff model, expected to be used for Energiø Bornholm, to all renewable energy (RE) electricity producers connected at the transmission level.

I must first note that according to the market directive, it is the collective electricity supply companies that develop tariff methods, and the Energy Regulatory Authority (Forsyningstilsynet) that approves them. This means that the Minister or the Parliament has very limited ability to dictate tariff designs.

The tariff pricing methods must, among other things, adhere to the principle of cost-reflectiveness, meaning they must reflect the costs incurred by the various categories of network users. In connection with this, Energinet has informed me that the general tariff model for producer payments specifically excludes electricity production connected to energy islands. This is because the standardized connection fee now applied for electricity production cannot, in a cost-reflective manner, accommodate the payment required for connection to energy islands. The transmission network at and near energy islands is of a special nature, as it includes both trade connections to foreign countries and specialized installations for connecting offshore wind, which also involves significantly higher investment costs compared to, for example, the connection of a typical offshore wind farm or larger solar park.

As a result, Energinet is currently developing a tariff financing model for Energinet’s costs related to energy islands. This model was sent for public consultation on May 3, 2023, with a response deadline of June 6, 2023. The draft tariff model proposes that the offshore wind connected to an energy island will be tariffed according to the costs it incurs. This draft includes, among other things, that electricity producers and consumers will share the financing of parts of Energinet’s costs using a distribution key specially developed for financing Energinet’s costs related to energy islands in order to allocate these costs in a cost-reflective manner.

Such a distribution key cannot be applied to tariffing other RE electricity producers, as they do not contribute to the financing of trade connections as part of their connection to the grid. This is because other RE electricity producers are not directly dependent on specific trade connections in their grid connection and the sale of their production, like the offshore wind connected at Energiø Bornholm.

1411. ID: 2388
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: DG Expertise
   Statement: The goal is to build two artificial islands off the coast of Denmark in the Baltic Sea. These islands will serve as hubs for renewable energy production, supplying power to the entire country and acting as centers for research and development in sustainable energy technologies. The Danish government also plans to export the energy produced to other European countries, fostering job creation and economic growth.

The two islands will each cover around 120,000 square meters and be located 80 and 100 kilometers from Denmark's coast. They will be equipped with large-scale wind turbines, solar panels, and other renewable energy technologies. By 2030, the project aims to generate approximately 10 GW of renewable electricity, enough to power about 10 million households across Europe. The project will be financed through a mix of public and private funds, with an initial budget of 125 million euros already allocated for the first phase of development.

1441. ID: 1839
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Michael Stoltze
   Statement: The transition from climate-damaging to climate-neutral energy sources is fraught with challenges, including the massive scale of the required infrastructure. Bornholm’s geographical position in a critical sea area for renewable energy delivery to Northern Europe places the island in the middle of a significant dilemma.

While we recognize the uncertain economic feasibility of these large-scale projects, we are particularly concerned about their potential impact on Bornholm’s nature and landscape. These are foundational values for Bornholm and the main reasons for its popularity, which must not be jeopardized.

As Danmarks Naturfredningsforening Bornholm, our primary goal is to protect and improve nature, the environment, and the landscape. We fully support the green transition to a society that avoids pollution, stabilizes the climate, preserves nature, and protects landscapes. A blanket rejection of all development, including wind turbines and solar farms, is not a viable option. Effective environmental solutions are essential to address pollution and climate change while maintaining the integrity of nature and the landscape.

For the massive land-based energy infrastructure planned on Bornholm, we demand the highest standards and will not compromise. This will be the largest construction project in Bornholm’s history, occupying a small percentage of the island’s area but having a visible impact due to the height of the structures. Therefore, it must be situated in a way that minimizes harm to nature and the landscape. The design should incorporate architecture, vegetation, and earthworks to integrate harmoniously into the surroundings.

The proposed location north of Søndre Landevej, although not without issues, is the best option available. The site is primarily agricultural land with low natural value, flat terrain, and a location sufficiently distant from the scenic south coast. While the project will affect farmland and buildings, the surrounding natural environment can be enhanced through thoughtful design. The plan includes low vegetation, bushes, and trees between the buildings, as well as tree lines and the restoration of a small stream, which will increase the area’s biodiversity compared to its current state.

However, we emphasize the need for varied-height earthen berms around the site. These berms will reduce the visual dominance of the large buildings and provide habitats for diverse flora and fauna by creating microclimates. Additionally, the berms can be used for walking trails, offering both scenic views and access to nature.

Nature and the landscape must not be sacrificed. This project is a significant opportunity to develop a solution that benefits Bornholm while serving as a national and international model for integrating renewable energy development with respect for nature and the landscape. This is the challenge we face, and we are committed to making it a success.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1470. ID: 1841
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Søren Møller Christensen
   Statement: I have been asked several times how it makes sense to produce power-to-x on Bornholm. Wouldn't it make much more sense to transport electricity to Copenhagen or Berlin and convert it into, for example, jet fuels in those locations, where there are also large cities with extensive district heating networks that can absorb the significant amounts of heat? It’s a logical question.

The issue, however, is that transporting electricity through cables is expensive, while transporting hydrogen through pipelines is cheaper. In other words, from an economic perspective, it makes the most sense to produce hydrogen as close to the energy source as possible. This is reflected in the fact that wind turbine manufacturers are working on developing turbines that, in the future, will produce hydrogen directly inside the turbine or on platforms near the turbines. In these turbines, most of the heat will be lost, but they are expected to be cost-effective because the electricity is converted to hydrogen very close to the energy source.

However, this type of turbine will not be used for Energy Island Bornholm, as the primary focus is on electricity production, and the new turbine type is not expected to be ready until the 2030s.

Regarding the question of why it is relevant to produce hydrogen on Bornholm, it is also worth noting that Bornholm is not the only community grappling with what power-to-x means for them. Green fuels, particularly hydrogen, are part of the vision in most places where there are plans for major expansions of wind and solar energy—and often, these are in smaller communities far from major cities. For example, this is also the case for the two other energy islands in the Baltic Sea, Gotland and Åland. Åland, in particular, is far along in its plans to produce hydrogen based on the 4–6 GW of offshore wind that can be developed in the waters around the archipelago.

I am often asked whether power-to-x makes economic sense. The think tank Kraka has, for example, published a report arguing that building a power-to-x industry in Denmark will require substantial financial support because green fuels are currently more expensive than fossil fuels. Both the question and the argument are logical, but they do not change the fact that power-to-x is an essential part of the solution to the climate crisis. Moreover, there is political recognition of the need to find ways to enable the commercial production of green fuels.

This can happen through support from the Danish state or the EU, which is already occurring today. In the future, it is also expected to happen through additional taxes based on the amount of CO₂ emitted by a particular type of production, making CO₂-neutral fuels more competitive compared to, for instance, coal and oil.

Whether power-to-x is supported directly through subsidies or indirectly through CO₂ taxes, the energy sector expects power-to-x to play a crucial role in the green transition. Furthermore, there is significant political focus in Denmark on making power-to-x a new area of national industrial strength.

1479. ID: 4831
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Job creation and innovation
   Actor: Claus M. Andersen
   Statement: This might be the most groundbreaking project we’ve landed in the 15 years we’ve hosted research and demonstration projects.

The Combined Heat and Power Plant on Skansevej in Rønne will soon house the Second Life for Powerplants project.

A number of European pioneers in energy technology have teamed up to solve one of the biggest challenges in sustainable transition: capturing and storing energy from solar and wind power, ensuring electricity and heat are available even on cloudy, windless days. The project budget is DKK 100 million, with EU support amounting to DKK 60 million.

The idea behind Second Life for Powerplants is to repurpose existing power plant technology while building on employees' skills. This means reusing the steam turbine, generator, control systems, and connections to the electricity grid and district heating network. The power plant will be equipped with three new storage technologies: a salt storage system, used electric vehicle batteries, and a high-tech flywheel battery. At the core of the concept is an advanced control software designed to ensure the availability of electricity and heat – even on overcast days with no wind.

"We will gain invaluable knowledge about how to handle and store solar and wind energy in the future – and how to effectively ensure balance in the electricity system. We will obtain solid insights into what it takes to fully utilize solar and wind power without significantly increasing costs for Bornholm’s residents. We will also get clear indications of the investments required to finally say goodbye to oil and phase out wood chips," I explained.

I also pointed out that the experiences gained from the project on Bornholm can be easily replicated elsewhere, making it much easier, cheaper, and faster to convert, for instance, a Polish coal power plant into a flexible energy storage facility for solar and wind power.

"The fact that we could land such a project on Bornholm might suggest that we should consider raising our expectations about the additional activity the Bornholm Energy Island will generate for the island," I concluded.

CONTROVERSY:
The Danish “Energy Island” projects

TEXT:
Offshore wind energy generation is more efficient than on land, to harness it you’d have to follow the wind. Ocean water currents offer a much higher energy density, at a stable rate, the technology is progressing, to harness you’d have to follow the currents. 
To make Hydrogen Green, sea water reverse osmosis and electrolysis equipment have to be close to an energy source, from here the idea of Energy Islands begins. 

Energy Islands should be near the winds, waves and currents. The Baltic Sea average depth is 50 m, the North Sea 90 m, the Mediterranean Sea 1,500 m, the Atlantic Ocean 3,600 m.

Energy Islands should be accessible all year long. Offshore rigs personnel have to go through extensive safety training to be allowed to make the trip by Helicopter or by Offshore Support Vessels, both ways are expensive and at high risk.
Energy Islands should cater for additional space when an Wind Farm expands; and permit ergonomic maintenance and replacement of equipment without the use of heavy lift Floating Marine Cranes and Floating Docks.

Energy Islands service and operations teams may range from dozens to hundreds. This team require fresh water supply, food supply, cold service water, hot service water, wastewater disposal, solid waste disposal and regular rotation.  Offshore supply and retrieval trips made by Offshore Supply Vessels is dangerous and expensive in high seas.

Supposing a nation wishes to build an Energy Island by backfilling into the sea within its economic water zone; the currents within this sea would have to be studied not to alter direction and affect neighboring nations, the sediments from the backfilling process would be carried to undesirable locations within the nation shoreline, or to neighboring shoreline, affecting marine fauna and flora. A thorough Environmental Impact Assessment should be endorsed by all nation stakeholders.
Assuming an EIA is approved, lets look at the backfilling process on a sandy bed at 50 m seawater depth. If the surface footprint of the island is to be 500m x 500m, the scour protection measures, whatever the method used, would have a footprint of around 600m x 600m at sea bed level. The offshore contracting operations would have to be carried out within the yearly calm season, if the entire operation, or the milestone target construction is not achieved within the first season, the sea would destroy and remove most of it before the next season.
 After completion, if a structural failure occurs, under rough sea conditions, repairs would have to wait till the calm season, at the risk of further uncontrollable damage.
Once such Energy Island is completed, installing equipment on top would follow any port procedures; if certain components need to be replaced, they would have to be lifted and transported onto a vessel.
While this enormous offshore marine contracting job maybe concluded at 50m depth, will let the reader imagine the 90m or 1,500m sea depth scenario feasibility.

A Floating Island is fabricated in a shipyard, launched to sea, tugged to the desired location, and anchored. The process is carried in a controlled environment, irrespective of sea state and sea depth.
While many Floating Island solutions are marketed, and most developers submitted their design to the UN Habitat in 2018 in a New York meeting, none of their literature is conclusive, most of it is at conceptual level. 
The only solution that passed Two Marine Societies design approval by Bureau Veritas  in 2005 and International Naval Survey Bureau in 2009, and a thorough Marine Society design, engineering, procurement and fabrication survey by INSB from 2009 till 2015 is the one made by Dr. Abdullah Daou, the founder of Beirut International Marine Industry and Commerce. 
Beirut International’s Floating Island first prototype was made in 1997, at a scale of 1:10 measuring 4m x 4m, was extensively tested in a make shift water basin, with better than expected stability results under high simulated waves condition.

In 2009 the fabrication of the first Floating Island made by Beirut International started in Lebanon. The substructure base 48m wide, by 76m long, 9m deep and weighing around 4,000 tons was being assembled in Tripoli Shipyard, while structural components where being fabricated in three other workshops in Lebanon by a team of 431 local technicians and engineers. 
While the fate of this structure was unfortunate, Ninety-Eight Million US Dollars were invested in the research, development and fabrication; a 70% completion rate was achieved, almost all drawings approved and stamped by INSB meeting SOLAS and other marine regulations. 
The learning curve is priceless. The technology is ready, far ahead of any contender. True, a full-scale prototype is yet to be made again and tested.


There is seven pros for building the energy islands.
A Floating Energy Island is modular, making it scalable to meet any Offshore Wind Farm expansion. If maintenance is requires, a module can be detached, tugged to a shipyard then re-connected.
The substructure of a Floating Energy Island is transparent to the sea, making it an artificial coral reef for marine life, and simultaneously providing anchoring points to install Water Current Energy makers. 
The waves are absorbed and damped by the Floating Energy Island, creating a calm water area at the rear port for Vessel to approach and dock at ease, allowing for safe and friendly access. 
Being a generator of Hydrogen, and having a large underwater space, it is an ideal location to develop sustainable fisheries, creating an additional export income.
Solid waste composting and wastewater treatment available technologies can make some agriculture a sustainable alternative to waste disposal.
The Hydrogen process being noiseless, and clean; a Yacht Club can be safe haven for yachts sailing across seas and oceans.

However the cons of building the islands are yet to be tested by our firm.

The Hydrogen Environment is relatively new. 
Stakeholders include: Shipping Companies, Energy Companies, Ports Logistics, Telecommunication, Reverse Osmosis Water Makers, Electroliser Makers, Wind Turbine makers, Wave Energy Makers, Current Energy Makers, Shipyards, Marine Offshore Contractors, Hydrogen Storage Solution Makers, Inverters, Controls, Aquaponics, Wastewater Treatment, Solid Waste Treatment… 
While some stakeholders are more advanced then the other, some at prototyping stage, other at maturity; a Floating Energy Island success needs their close collaboration. A fresh firm in the Legal field is trying to advise stakeholders to join efforts and Joint Venture to make such infrastructure and energy concepts a needed reality to meet a Marine Decarbonization.

1500. ID: 1871
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Job creation and innovation
   Actor: Stig Westermann
   Statement: What can we expect from the business development on the island in connection with the Bornholm Energy Island, and not least, what do we want as Bornholm residents? In the Unity List, we are positive about the Energy Island, but we would like to ask questions about what Bornholm as a society will get out of it, and not least what might “come with it”, so to speak. With the Energy Island, we will have offshore wind turbines, cables to be laid, an even very large building - which will hopefully be “wrapped up nicely” - and some surplus heat, which may be used in our district heating system. When the turbines are spinning, we will undoubtedly also have a number of good jobs in connection with servicing them. Perhaps we will also get electricity for Bornholm, that is not yet completely clear.

During the construction itself, we will also have a lot of activity, which of course can and should benefit Bornholm. But we will also have four to six years of tremendous “logistics and construction chaos”. This very large project must in no way affect our current business community. Industry, agriculture and tourism will still be important elements in the business development on Bornholm. Wouldn't it therefore be very reasonable for us as a society to jointly make a "License To Operate" - that is, a "something for something" agreement with the state? We don't just want to end up as "a big power outlet" for the rest of Denmark/Europe. This something could, for example, be in the form of cheap electricity for the people of Bornholm, permanent housing, upgrading and maintenance of the road network, extra capacity on the ferry, green education or something completely different?

We have tried Bornholm as a test island before, and in fact we are quite good at it. So we in the Unity List will initially view this positively. Then we have CIP, which wants to build two wind farms east of Bornholm. From what we understand, CIP wants to use all the electricity for a PtX plant, where they will produce hydrogen, which may be sold from the Port of Rønne or transported away from the island in some other way? If CIP were to succeed with their project, it would mean another large plant - perhaps 20-30 hectares - on the island. When producing hydrogen, you need water - a lot of water - about 6 million cubic meters per year.

Another positive area could be cheap heat. Such a PtX plant produces a lot of heat in the process. Enough to heat all our homes several times over. Of course, this should benefit us all if necessary

In the current municipal council, more than a year after we took office - for several reasons - we have unfortunately not yet succeeded in creating a vision plan for Bornholm. It is high time this happened, not least in light of the Energy Island project. It was also a theme that was discussed on the trips to Jutland. All the participants missed having a direction set out - read vision plan - from the island's politicians.

1513. ID: 4838
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: Kraka Economics
   Statement: It is concerning when civil servants take a stance on politically sensitive issues in public debates. Recently, Energinet's Director of Megaprojects, Hanne Storm Edlefsen, has again defended the energy island projects, both of which have enormous socio-economic deficits and thus put Danes at a disadvantage. The poor economy has even led economic experts to recommend dropping the project unless positive socio-economic benefits can be demonstrated. There is no doubt that the project is highly challenged.

It muddies the debate when a high-ranking civil servant in this article on dr.dk and in other contexts neglects valid arguments, such as large billion-dollar expenses, and instead presents meaningless arguments like the project's long lifespan. This has nothing to do with the matter: Projects with negative socio-economics put Danes at a disadvantage and should be dropped, regardless of the project's lifespan.

It actually matters when a director of Energinet speaks out because Energinet's employees rightly have a reputation as impartial, objective, and professionally competent people, and therefore it is extremely toxic for the debate that a director repeatedly appears as the biggest lobbyist for the energy island projects.

DR's story is precisely about what we at Kraka Economics have long warned against: The cost of dropping Energy Island Bornholm grows every day politicians hesitate to bury the project.

700 million DKK has so far been spent on, among other things, preliminary investigations and project maturation, and the bill is expected to gradually rise to 1.2 billion DKK.

It is not in itself strange or criticizable that it costs money to prepare the establishment of large, expensive construction projects. But it is, however, criticizable to continue pouring money into the hole that Energy Island Bornholm represents. There is a high probability that the project will not be completed at all because politicians have allocated 14 billion DKK less for it than the Danish Energy Agency expects is needed.

The likely waste of money will only get worse as soon as the first subcontracts (e.g., for cables) are awarded in early 2025, because these contracts are, of course, not free to tear up when it is ultimately found that the project cannot be completed within the established support framework.

The project's lifespan is completely irrelevant in this context. And it is concerning if the debate is derailed with nonsensical arguments.

1521. ID: 4982
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: Brian Vad Mathiesen
   Statement: I believe that the Energy Island project at Bornholm is highly complex and that recent economic criticisms, such as the report from Kraka Economics entitled "Energiø Bornholm: En økonomisk katastrofe i slowmotion," although valid in highlighting economic challenges, only address well-known issues and do not offer solutions for enhancing profitability or ensuring regional energy security in the Baltic Sea. I point out that the report, funded by the Novo Nordisk Foundation and presented at the annual conference organized by the Danish Economic Councils, largely criticizes offshore wind in general rather than addressing the specific design issues of the Bornholm energy island project. I insist that to make the project economically viable, we must continue to pursue our renewable energy targets and transition to a consumption-driven system in which investments in the lowest-cost renewable energy are stimulated by growing demand. I argue that it is crucial to integrate innovative technologies, such as Power-to-X solutions and data centers, to absorb surplus production and reduce fossil fuel usage in high-emission sectors. I also emphasize that the Bornholm project is not solely about securing Denmark’s energy supply, but is equally important for enhancing Europe’s overall energy security. I acknowledge that the economic critiques are justified, yet we must consider alternative strategies, such as connecting the energy island to networks in Sweden or Poland to lower costs. I further note that while challenges exist, the project is likely to be implemented with the necessary adjustments and potential delays, similar to the positive adjustments seen in the shelved North Sea energy island project, which indicates that designs can be adapted to meet economic realities. Ultimately, I maintain that the mixed economic performance of the Bornholm energy island is more about the design of the wind park than about the fundamental viability of offshore wind technology in the Baltic region.

The exhibition is a prelude to the international conference Baltic Energy Island Summit 2023, which gathers companies, universities, and authorities from near and far. At the center of it all is Energy Island Bornholm and how we are jointly developing Bornholm and the Baltic Sea into a center for green energy.

Baltic Energy Island is a partnership between Bornholm Regional Municipality, Ørsted, Campus Bornholm, CRT - Center for Regional and Tourism Research, Port of Rønne, the Technical University of Denmark, Bornholm’s Energy & Supply, Business Center Bornholm, Offshore Center Bornholm, Energy Cluster Denmark, Siemens Gamesa, Copenhagen Capacity, and Energinet.

1544. ID: 4844
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: Kraka Economics
   Statement: Minister finally opens up to dropping Energy Island Bornholm

Perhaps there is finally hope for Danish taxpayers who have long faced a bill of 31.5 billion DKK for an energy island with negative socio-economic impact.

According to an article in Jyllands-Posten, Minister for Climate, Energy, and Utilities Lars Aagaard will now engage with the parties behind the original decision on Energy Island Bornholm. Together with them, he will discuss the large financial gaps and whether to find the missing funds or ultimately drop the energy island.

The background is the recent failed offshore wind auction, where no developers wanted to bid on the 3 GW in the North Sea. The auction was supposed to secure a substantial part of the funding for Energy Island Bornholm, and it is among other things these missing billions that the minister now has to find together with the agreement group.

But it seems that the parties behind the energy island may need to find even more money, as the bill will likely only have grown when the Danish Energy Agency soon releases new calculations of the project's already poor economics.

Neither do the developers themselves believe that the project can be realized, according to Bornholms Tidende, which has spoken with more than 20 stakeholders in the project. It is simply impossible to make the project economically viable as it stands today, the industry reports.

At Kraka Economics, we urge Lars Aagaard to take the discussions he himself proposes with the agreement group as soon as possible. It is time to make the only responsible decision and drop the project in its current form. It is okay to become wiser—especially when it concerns bills for Danes that probably now exceed 40 billion DKK for a project with poor socio-economic impact.

In this report, we shed light on the turbulent process that has been around Energiø Bornholm so far and the many economic and political risks associated with the further process if the agreement is maintained. In addition, we highlight the absurdity of spending a two-digit billion sum on an energy island, when other offshore wind can be built without support, and when the electricity must also be primarily exported to Germany, so that Danish taxpayers end up paying for Germany's green transition. 

The report clearly exposes the many problems with the project, and on that basis we strongly urge that the project be dropped or at least postponed until a better, more cost-effective solution is found. The billions can be used to advantage on a faster, real green transition.”

1619. ID: 6540
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Lars Tornsberg
   Statement: The plans for a large Energy Island and perhaps 700 offshore wind turbines will mean that a significant part of the North Sea will be occupied. It is already an area where the fishermen have had their jobs for many years. If the space for fishing is not taken into account, it can create major challenges. 

Firstly, fishing risks that the areas traditionally fished in become inaccessible. This can mean having to sail further to find fishing grounds, which will increase costs and make it more difficult to maintain a sustainable operation. 

In addition, the new structures in the sea, such as the Energy Island and the sea turbines, can negatively affect fish stocks. For example, changes in the seabed and new installations can change the natural movements and habitats of fish. 

It is therefore important that the needs of fishing are taken into account in the planning of the Energy Island and the many offshore wind turbines. The fishermen hope that the authorities will listen to the concerns and work together with the fisheries representatives to find solutions that can ensure both sustainable energy development and continued viable fishing.

1672. ID: 6696
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: Rasmus Errboe
   Statement: Together with ATP, Ørsted proposes a modular approach to constructing the North Sea Energy Island. The proposal involves initially building a smaller, enclosed artificial island that can be expanded over time using additional modules. These modules, such as components to transmit offshore wind power to land, can be added as technology advances or needs change. This approach is akin to building with LEGO bricks, starting with a foundation and expanding incrementally.  

The modular design emphasizes flexibility and adaptability, aligning with the long-term goal of achieving a 10-gigawatt capacity by 2040 to supply green electricity to 10 million households.  

Ørsted views this method as an efficient way to manage the island's construction and scalability while responding to evolving technological and energy demands.

1697. ID: 5488
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: The Danish Energy Island in the North Sea is a visionary project that can contribute significantly to Europe’s green transition and energy security. However, implementing such an unprecedented project involves many challenges, financial risks, and difficult decisions. From the beginning, political consensus across the Danish Parliament has been that the project must be economically responsible. The initial cost of over 50 billion DKK for the state was never the intention, and adjustments to reduce the price were announced last summer.

A key purpose of the energy island is to export electricity to other countries. Collaboration with Belgium was pursued, but we could not agree on a cost-benefit distribution that was fair and acceptable to Denmark. Should a future Belgian government propose a more balanced agreement, Denmark remains open to discussions.

In the meantime, we have engaged with other partners, particularly Germany, which has shown significant interest in connecting to the energy island. Our dialogue with Germany is advanced, and we are now prioritizing a partnership where the energy island will connect to both Denmark and Germany through electrical cables. Germany’s needs, including capacity and timelines, will influence the project’s realization as they are essentially a customer investing in this green project.

Revised plans and partnerships mean the timeline for the energy island’s completion will be extended. However, this new direction with Germany could make the project more financially feasible for Denmark. The next steps involve concrete planning to create a foundation for political decision-making, which is currently in progress.

1698. ID: 5490
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Troels Ranis
   Statement: Energiø Bornholm is a significant project that will provide green electricity to 3-4 million households and reduce CO₂ emissions by over 3 million tons annually. However, its greatest importance lies in its visionary and innovative role, contributing to three key areas: climate, industry, and security policy.

Energiø Bornholm serves as a catalyst for the European green transition, especially in fostering the development of future energy islands, such as those in the North Sea. These islands are essential to achieving the EU’s goal of 300 GW offshore wind energy by 2050 in a cost-effective and efficient manner. The project exemplifies Denmark's original ambition to be a visionary leader, driving a greener, safer Europe less reliant on fossil energy, particularly from Russia.

Industrially, Energiø Bornholm offers a testing and innovation platform that can help Danish companies maintain a technological leadership position in energy island development and secure the next generation of Danish wind energy advancements. This is crucial for Denmark’s competitiveness in the global green industry, which is currently under pressure.

From a security policy perspective, Energiø Bornholm directly strengthens Europe’s energy self-sufficiency by acting as a hub linking electricity markets in the southern Baltic Sea. It also demonstrates a scalable model for expanding offshore wind and electricity trading, particularly in the North Sea, making it a cornerstone of Europe’s future energy supply and security strategies.

The societal and economic value of Energiø Bornholm is broader than immediate costs and revenues. Although initial calculations from 2023 show a 4 billion DKK deficit if Europe meets its climate goals, these calculations fail to account for key benefits, such as Denmark’s strengthened technological leadership in wind energy, the economic potential of a future cable to Poland, EU funding opportunities, and increased energy security. Additional benefits include opportunities for Power-to-X production, connections to Bornholm, job creation on the island, and broader strategic advantages.

Energiø Bornholm is not just a project with immediate economic returns; it is a long-term investment in critical infrastructure that will drive economic growth, enhance energy security, and solidify Denmark’s strategic position as a global wind energy leader.

1733. ID: 5256
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Development & innovation opportunities on Bornholm
   Actor: Center for Regional and Tourism Research
   Statement: An analysis by CRT - Center for Regional and Tourism Research - concludes that Energy Island Bornholm has the potential to contribute significantly to reaching the political goal of 42,000 residents on Bornholm by 2030, but only if a Power-to-X facility is established.

CRT outlines three scenarios in its analysis:
1. **The Expected Scenario:** Represents the base case tied to Energy Island Bornholm’s construction and does not include any additional facilities or roles.
2. **The Possible Scenario:** Adds more jobs and new residents by making Bornholm an installation hub for offshore wind turbines during their construction phase, resulting in 100 additional jobs and 120 new residents.
3. **The Extended Scenario:** Builds upon the first two scenarios and introduces a Power-to-X facility on Bornholm, creating an additional 410 jobs and attracting 480 more residents.

In its calculations, CRT considers not only direct jobs created by the Energy Island project but also indirect effects, such as increased demand for local goods, restaurants, and childcare services. For example, Rønne Havn would need more staff to service wind turbines, and local businesses, such as food vendors, would hire additional employees to meet the rising demand.

Additionally, CRT estimates that there will be 5,300 temporary full-time equivalent positions created during the construction period leading up to 2030. However, CRT has not accounted for the long-term growth of the broader green industry on Bornholm, which could emerge from new business and research opportunities related to Energy Island Bornholm.

While it is impossible to quantify how many green companies and jobs might realistically develop as a result of these investments, CRT emphasizes that it is equally unrealistic to assume that no new energy-related businesses will emerge. Consequently, Energy Island Bornholm could create even more jobs than currently estimated.

1734. ID: 5262
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: Based on an environmental assessment and public consultation responses, the Danish Energy Agency has determined that the Plan for Program Energy Island Bornholm can be adopted, allowing the energy island project to proceed.

The Energy Island Bornholm plan establishes the framework for an energy island consisting of an offshore wind farm south of Bornholm and high-voltage facilities on Bornholm and Zealand. The Energy Island will have a capacity of up to 3.8 GW, making the Energy Island crucial for phasing out fossil fuel energy sources.

The Danish Energy Agency has made several spatial adjustments to the planning areas to accommodate environmental concerns and area restrictions, including bird protection areas, defense areas, and shipping routes. The Danish Energy Agency held multiple public meetings in 2021, 2022, and 2023 during consultation periods where citizens, stakeholders, and authorities submitted ideas, proposals, concerns, and questions about the draft plan and environmental assessment.

While the plan establishes the overall framework for future construction projects for Energy Island Bornholm, the plan alone does not authorize construction of facilities. The Danish Energy Agency's decision can be appealed to the Energy Board of Appeal within a 4-week period until June 10, 2024.

1736. ID: 5266
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: Kraka Economics
   Statement: The Energy Island Bornholm project is economically risky and underfunded. It has the potential to become a "slow-motion economic catastrophe." We recommend dropping the project before costs spiral out of control. 

Our analysis shows that the project is unlikely to attract bids to install offshore wind turbines because the expected income of 87 billion kroner from electricity sales over the project's lifespan is insufficient to cover costs unless the government increases the subsidy cap from 17.6 billion kroner to 31.5 billion kroner. Without this increase, the project is not financially attractive. 

To make the project viable with the current subsidy cap, electricity revenue would need to increase by 16.9 billion kroner, reaching 103.9 billion kroner. If the project were to proceed without any government support, the required revenue would rise to 125.3 billion kroner. This level of income is highly unlikely under current market conditions.

There is significant risk that the Energy Island Bornholm project cannot be realized within the current subsidy framework, and it is doubtful that companies will bid to install the wind turbines. If no bids are made, politicians face two choices: either abandon the project entirely or increase the subsidy to the necessary 31.5 billion kroner. While raising the subsidy might deliver the energy island, it contradicts the original intention of making the project economically self-sufficient.

Abandoning the project also carries financial consequences because the project is structured as smaller contracts. Terminating these contracts will result in substantial costs, even if the project ultimately fails to materialize. This financial risk makes it crucial to reconsider the feasibility of continuing with the Energy Island Bornholm project.

As of this year, the total cost is estimated at 31.5 billion kroner, but the latest price estimate is currently known only to the Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities and the government. The tender and construction of the offshore wind turbines are pending Energinet’s tender for electrical equipment. The Ministry acknowledges that time pressures, economic challenges, and market conditions—such as an overheated global market for electrical equipment, rising interest rates, and inflation—are impacting both delivery timelines and costs. The Ministry cannot yet provide a new price estimate. The overall project economy is under review, and once finalized, the minister will convene the agreement parties for further discussions.

The project could be made cheaper by accelerating the construction of some of the offshore wind turbines whose power will be routed through the energy island.

1742. ID: 5360
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Belgium’s energy island
   Actor: Private person
   Statement: Belgium has started constructing the world’s first artificial energy island, Princess Elisabeth Island, located 45 kilometers off the Belgian coast in the North Sea. This project is a significant step forward in renewable energy infrastructure, aiming to enhance renewable energy usage and facilitate international energy exchange.  

The island, supported by a €100 million grant from the EU’s COVID-19 recovery fund, will feature integrated HVDC and HVAC systems to distribute energy from offshore wind farms to the grid. Hybrid interconnectors will enable connections with wind farms and energy trade between countries.  

The construction involves innovative methods, including 2.3 million cubic meters of sand and concrete caissons to form its base and walls. Strategically, this project reduces Belgium’s reliance on fossil fuels and positions the North Sea as a hub for Europe’s energy independence.  

The island’s physical structure is expected to be completed by 2026, with operations commencing in 2030. This groundbreaking initiative underscores Belgium’s leadership in renewable energy and its commitment to sustainability and energy security.

1753. ID: 5809
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: The Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: We have, based on an environmental assessment of the plan and feedback received during consultations, determined that it is possible to approve the Plan for the Energy Island Bornholm Program. This means that work on the energy island can continue.

The Plan for the Energy Island Bornholm Program establishes the framework for the upcoming energy island on and off the coast of Bornholm. Energy Island Bornholm will consist of an offshore wind farm south of Bornholm as well as high-voltage facilities on Bornholm and Zealand. The energy island will have a capacity of up to 3.8 GW, thereby playing a significant role in phasing out fossil energy sources.

We have made several area adjustments to the planning zones to account for environmental conditions and area restrictions in the region, such as bird protection areas, defense zones, and shipping routes.

As part of the process, we organized a series of public meetings in 2021, 2022, and 2023 during the consultation periods, where citizens, stakeholders, and authorities submitted ideas, proposals, concerns, and questions about the draft plan and environmental assessment. With this plan, we set the overarching framework for future construction projects for Energy Island Bornholm.

We emphasize that the plan alone does not authorize the establishment of facilities. Our decision can be appealed to the Energy Board of Appeal within a 4-week period until June 10, 2024.

1761. ID: 5867
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Bornholm Museum
   Statement: Before construction for Energy Island Bornholm can commence, a crucial part of Denmark’s history must be safeguarded. Bornholms Museum has initiated the largest archaeological excavations ever undertaken on the island, spanning 35 hectares to uncover Denmark’s cultural heritage.

Preliminary studies of the area designated for the land-based facilities of Energy Island Bornholm have already provided a remarkable overview of the cultural landscape, dating back as far as 6,000 years. Artifacts from the Neolithic period to the Viking Age could shed new light on Bornholm’s role in culture, trade, and religion within the Baltic region. From flint tools and rock carvings to settlements and burial sites, the archaeological finds will be documented and preserved for future generations.

The excavations are being carried out in phases over several years. The first phase focuses on an 8-hectare area in the southern part of the site, where four settlements have been identified. A team of six archaeologists will conduct deeper investigations to uncover additional traces of habitation, tools, and other historical remnants. Energinet, as the developer, is funding the archaeological work, which is being led by Bornholms Museum.

1773. ID: 5901
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: René Danielsson
   Statement: MAY 2025 BE THE YEAR OF HONESTY! 🤞🏻  

Politicians have a tendency to sugarcoat things. That’s also the case on Bornholm.  

We constantly hear Social Democrats, Conservatives, and others claim that if Energy Island Bornholm happens, everything will be great.  

They call it business policy and present the Energy Island as Bornholm's great savior, which will free us from austerity measures and equalization payments.  

But is it really? 🧐🤔  

Bornholm receives 1.3 billion kroner in equalization payments and subsidies annually.  

Even the most optimistic analyses suggest that the Energy Island would yield a return of around 60 million kroner by approximately 2036—and that’s if the PtX industry gets off the ground.  

Therefore, it’s simply a lie to present the Energy Island as something that will make Bornholm economically sustainable. For that to happen, we’d need over 14,000 new residents with an average income of 350,000 kroner—about 64,000 more than the current average income on Bornholm. If we stick to the current average income, the number rises to over 17,000 new residents! 😳🤯

Bornholm will NEVER be economically self-sufficient. We are dependent on equalization payments—unfortunately.  

However, there is tremendous economic potential in investing in the people of Bornholm. For example, improving the well-being of just 10 percent of public school students could generate a minimum of 83 million kroner in municipal revenue over a lifetime. On top of that, we would see reduced expenses as a result of improved well-being.  

The future of Bornholm depends on its people and their welfare—not on fanciful projects that divert funding away from what we know works.  

But to start, politicians need to tell the truth as it is—not as they wish it were.  

What do you think?

1775. ID: 5953
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: The Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The Danish Energy Agency has reported on the socioeconomic impact assessments for different configurations of the Energy Island Bornholm under various scenarios. The Energy Island Bornholm project includes offshore wind farms, a transformer station on Bornholm, and grid connections to Denmark and Germany. Despite considerable uncertainty about future developments, the central socioeconomic estimates are negative across all scenarios, ranging from -4 billion DKK to -17 billion DKK.

The project is also expected to require public subsidies amounting to 31.5 billion DKK during the first approximately 20 years of the energy island's lifespan. Of this, 17.6 billion DKK was politically approved in May 2023. This approved subsidy will be financed through expected revenues from the auction of 6 GW offshore wind capacity (8.7 billion DKK), the Green Fund (4.9 billion DKK), and future fiscal space (4.0 billion DKK). An additional subsidy need of approximately 14 billion DKK has arisen due to the anticipated unprofitability of the offshore wind farms associated with the energy island, and no concrete financing has yet been identified for this amount.

Given the negative socioeconomic outlook, the Energy Island Bornholm project should be reconsidered. The socioeconomic assessment does not include several effects that are difficult to quantify, such as energy security and potential Power-to-X production. It is recommended that a comprehensive socioeconomic analysis be conducted, incorporating as many effects as possible. If it cannot be demonstrated that the project yields a socioeconomic surplus, the project should be abandoned.

1777. ID: 5975

Similarly, the production of ammonia, methanol, and the use of carbon dioxide (CO2) as a feedstock for fuel and chemical production are proven technologies. However, there is ongoing innovation in Power-to-X (PtX) technologies aimed at enhancing efficiency, reducing costs, and improving safety. These advancements focus on developing new catalysts, improving materials, and optimizing process integration to increase the viability and feasibility of PtX technologies.

The success of PtX projects depends on proper safety protocols and comprehensive risk assessments. These protocols address critical aspects such as the handling, production, storage, and transportation of fuels and chemicals. Risk assessments are crucial for identifying and mitigating potential vulnerabilities, reducing rework costs, ensuring regulatory compliance, and selecting appropriate security partners and protocols. Given the complexity of energy projects and the involvement of multiple stakeholders, these assessments form a foundational element for the successful and sustainable implementation of PtX initiatives. They help achieve project objectives while ensuring secure and efficient operations, ultimately advancing the overall potential of PtX technologies.

1792. ID: 5675
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Dr. Elmar Friedrich
   Statement: The development of energy islands in the German North Sea is a transformative project that I fully support. These islands, located over 100 kilometers from the German shoreline and spanning an area the size of approximately 70 soccer fields, will play a critical role in advancing Germany's energy transition. 

The energy islands will enable the local production of green hydrogen powered by nearby offshore wind farms, reducing dependency on foreign energy, cutting green hydrogen costs, and minimizing the need for extensive grid expansion. They will provide flexibility by delivering electricity when needed and producing and storing green hydrogen during periods of surplus electricity.

The islands will also serve as hubs for efficient transmission infrastructure for offshore wind farms, resulting in significant cost savings and increased operational efficiency. Additionally, the islands will address health and safety challenges by hosting emergency medical centers, ensuring offshore workers receive timely assistance regardless of weather conditions.

For operation and maintenance of offshore wind farms, the islands will eliminate the need for technicians to live on Service Operation Vessels (SOVs) for weeks, offering a safer and more comfortable work environment. They will also enhance the protection of critical infrastructure at sea, providing better monitoring and defense capabilities.

The islands will be designed to support biodiversity, creating eco-friendly environments that benefit marine and terrestrial life. Moreover, the project is expected to generate over 10,000 jobs, benefiting coastal communities and other regions across the supply chain.

I am excited to lead this initiative with Copenhagen Offshore Partners and Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, confident that it will bring economic, environmental, and strategic benefits to Germany.

   Statement: I hereby submit a legislative proposal to modify the investment screening law and gas supply law. The investment screening law changes introduce an earlier screening timeline for certain cases, specifically to enable greater parallel processing between the new EU foreign subsidy screening (FSR) and investment screening for offshore wind tenders and other major public energy projects.

The proposal's late submission is due to the urgency of clarifying the screening process before the upcoming offshore wind tenders, including the already initiated Bornholm Energy Island electrical equipment tender. The law should enter into force on July 1, 2024.
